To bridge this gap, we introduce ViBMR, to the best of our knowledge, the first large-scale multi-sequence brain MRI dataset paired with routine Vietnamese clinical reports, comprising 3,649 patients and 11,875 MRI series across T1, T2, FLAIR, and contrast-enhanced T1 sequences. Building on ViBMR, we establish a comprehensive evaluation setup for brain MRI report generation, covering representative medical vision-language models, multi-sequence inputs, and feature aggregation strategies. The results provide key insights into dataset characteristics and model behavior, while demonstrating the necessity of native low-resource clinical datasets for reliable Vietnamese-origin brain MRI report generation. Our dataset and baseline models will be released for non-commercial research.

[633] arXiv:2610.29907 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Benchmarking Large Language Models for Detecting Satirical Code-Mixed Sentences
Răzvan-Alexandru Smădu, Ioana Buhnila, Daniela Tanase, Dumitru-Clementin Cercel, Florin Pop, Mihaela-Claudia Cercel
Comments: 35 pages, 8 figures
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Code-switching is a natural linguistic phenomenon, yet its impact on high-level reasoning tasks remains largely unexplored in under-resourced languages like Romanian. Natural language processing tasks, such as satire detection, rely heavily on nuanced cultural and syntactic cues that large language models struggle to capture. In this paper, we investigate four methods (i.e., random replacement, phrase translation, dependency parsing, and large language models) for generating synthetic code-mixed Romanian sentences with English, German, French, and Italian. We start with an existing dataset for satire detection, compiled from Romanian news articles and annotated at the sentence level by humans, and augment it with over 600k samples, namely CS-SeLeRoSa. We provide an in-depth analysis of the dataset generation process. Then, we evaluate several multilingual large language models across zero-shot, chain-of-thought, and fine-tuning regimes on both the synthetic corpus and a human-adjudicated gold benchmark, namely CS-SeLeRoSa-Gold. While older open models suffer substantial degradation (dropping to 37%-55% macro-F1), newer models like Gemma 4 31B achieve 68.1% zero-shot, rivaling frontier models like GPT-5 mini (69.5%). Furthermore, fine-tuning significantly reduces formatting errors and improves the results, increasing Gemma 4 31B to 77.5% on CS-SeLeRoSa and 72.6% on the gold standard, outperforming frontier zero-shot baselines.

[634] arXiv:2610.29913 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Asking a Multimodal LLM Whether Someone Fell: Zero-Shot Screening of Low-Resolution Thermal Video in a Laboratory and an Occupied Home
Marcos Junca (Senecta Inc.), Mauro Junca (Senecta Inc.)
Comments: 13 pages, 6 figures. Data: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Thermal cameras can watch over older people living alone without capturing faces, and multimodal large language models (LLMs) can judge a short video without task-specific training. We evaluate a production multimodal LLM, Gemini 3.8 Flash at temperature 0, as the decision stage of an event-triggered fall screener, used exactly as a deployed prototype uses it: one request per short thermal clip, with its sound track when there is one, and its predecessor Gemini 3.7 Flash on the same requests. On 438 staged falls and 563 non-fall windows that we located by hand in a public 32x24 thermal dataset, the deployed request called 69% of the held-out subjects' falls (67% over all subjects; bed falls excluded) and none of 499 non-fall windows, including people lying on the floor and getting up. Over 76 h of ordinary life in an occupied room, recorded at 160x120 with sound, it called none of 395 clips a fall (95% upper bound 1.2 false alarms per day) and caught 4 of the 9 staged falls the camera could see. One cautionary sentence in the prompt ("a person who goes out of view ... is not a fall") accounted for many of the misses: removing it raised sensitivity on the held-out subjects from 69% to 83% on 3.8 Flash and from 80% to 92% on Gemini 3.7 Flash, and in the home from 4 to 9 of the 9 visible falls, with no false call in ordinary living but at the price of calling deliberate lie-downs a fall. Sensitivity collapsed at 8x6 pixels (34%); identical requests disagreed on 4% of windows; and when the model called a fall, its explanation placed it within a second of the annotated landing 99% of the time. Two conventional detectors trained on the laboratory data caught nearly every held-out laboratory fall but raised 14.2 and 23.9 false alarms per day in the home. We release the frame-level fall annotations of the public dataset and every model answer on it.

[635] arXiv:2610.29915 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CausalAlign: Causal Alignment of Video Generation Models for Consistent Ego-Motion
Kai Zhu, Yintianrun Zhang, Shuwei Jiang, Ruolin Zuo, Yixin Chen, Duomin Wang, Miao Liu, Yin Li, Daquan Zhou, Yiwu Zhong
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Diffusion-based video generation models (VGMs) can produce visually plausible videos, yet their camera ego-motion often drifts over long horizons. Camera ego-motion determines how the viewpoint changes between frames and is essential for maintaining consistent geometry and trajectories. To address this problem, we propose CausalAlign, a causal alignment framework with two components. First, we diagnose how precise ego motion is represented, used, and retained within VGMs using linear probes and causal interventions, revealing a rise-and-fall pattern during denoising. Second, we strengthen ego-motion state in VGM by aligning the representations at the identified layers to a 3D foundation model through delta-token space. This space encodes the changes between consecutive frames, allowing the alignment to focus on ego-motion dynamics rather than static scene content. With Wan2.2 fine-tuned on DL3DV and RealEstate10K, CausalAlign can largely improve motion accuracy, geometric consistency, and temporal smoothness, while preserving visual quality. For example, it improves geometric consistency by more than 20% relative to the base model. Moreover, with the fine-tuned VGM, CausalAlign improves the success rate of world action models (WAMs) by 10 points on mobile manipulation tasks of RoboCasa365 benchmark. Overall, CausalAlign improves ego-motion consistency in diffusion-based VGMs and yields noticeable gains in embodied models.

[636] arXiv:2610.29918 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Preventing Model Extraction in Contextual Linear Optimization
Adam N. Elmachtoub, Tianyi Lin, Wenxuan Liu
Comments: 25 pages, 11 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Consider a contextual linear optimization problem, where a predict-then-optimize (PTO) system returns optimal decisions without revealing the cost vectors used in its downstream linear program. Our focus is on how to prevent attackers, who can submit context queries, from extracting the underlying prediction model. Although the cost-to-decision map is many-to-one, observations across contexts can reveal the underlying prediction model. For linear models, we provide sufficient conditions where the attacker can learn the model up to positive scaling by only observing the decision. These conditions motivate an adaptive attack that alternates inverse optimization with boundary sampling, i.e., using context queries leading to decision boundaries of the current attacker model. To prevent extraction, we propose a mechanism that perturbs decisions only when the predicted cost vector is near a decision boundary. We establish a regret bound in terms of the perturbation radius. For the attackers that fit the defended responses as optimal decisions under the evaluation distribution, we also prove a lower bound on expected extraction error. Experiments on synthetic instances and real data quantify the security-performance trade-off of the defense mechanism and illustrate that our defense can increase the extraction error.

[637] arXiv:2610.29922 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Unintended Side Effects of Value Training in LLMs
Siddhesh Pawar, Chen Cecilia Liu, Anna Korhonen, Isabelle Augenstein
Comments: 37 pages, 31 figures, 26 tables
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

As LLMs are increasingly deployed in value-sensitive contexts, aligning them with human values has emerged as a post-training objective in NLP, aimed at instilling additional values and guiding model behaviour. However, current evaluations remain narrow. Because values are interconnected, it is unclear how fine-tuning for specific values alters unrelated capabilities and behaviours. In this work, we adapt four instruction-tuned LLMs across individual Hofstede's value dimensions and evaluate them on both cross-value transfer and broader behaviours. We find that value-specific training produces unintended side effects on untrained values, risk preferences, social cognition, and safety traits. Consequently, we suggest that value alignment after post-training should incorporate broader behavioral evaluations, and we highlight the need to investigate where additional value training might best fit into the pipeline.

[638] arXiv:2610.29924 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Geospatial Dynamics of Online Attention to Nuclear Power in Japan Before and After Fukushima
Yifan Sun, Ken Kurosaki, Benjamin C. McLellan
Comments: 11 pages, 5 figures
Subjects: Social and Information Networks (cs.SI)

Nuclear power is increasingly seen as necessary for sustainable development, but this role depends on informed public engagement and support. Building this support requires understanding what citizens want to know, as reflected in their spontaneous online searches. To map this demand, we present the first long-term (2004-2024), prefecture-level analysis of Google Trends data on nuclear power in Japan. The results indicate that in routine periods, search interest followed a host-locality pattern, being significantly higher in prefectures hosting nuclear plants, with little spillover to their neighbors. Immediately after the Fukushima Daiichi accident in March 2011, this pattern changed, and interest instead declined with distance from Fukushima, before the host-locality pattern returned from 2012. During March 2011, searches leaned heavily toward general and live information rather than guidance on what to do. Their framing also varied with proximity, as those near Fukushima prioritized live updates and formal countermeasures, while others leaned toward background information and personal-scale questions. These patterns and the shift between them provide a behavioral evidence base for designing communication strategies in Japan and countries weighing the use of nuclear power. More broadly, the finding that searches vary with proximity can inform public communication in other geographically anchored crises.

[639] arXiv:2610.29925 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Privacy in Context Is Being Overlooked in the Age of General-Purpose LLMs
Prakhar Ganesh, Yash More, Marco Romanelli, Ferdinando Fioretto, Golnoosh Farnadi
Comments: Accepted at Personalization in the Era of Large Foundation Models Workshop @ AAAI 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

As large language models (LLMs) continue to grow in scope and capability, privacy concerns are on the rise. Since users increasingly interact with a single general-purpose system across many distinct contexts, there is a natural tendency to pursue a one-size-fits-all solution to privacy. Unfortunately, this overlooks a crucial insight from decades of privacy research: privacy is inherently contextual. In this paper, we argue that existing work in prompt privacy is drifting towards attempts to design a unified framework, which is highly misleading and can foster a false sense of security. Furthermore, we argue that even future work in this direction needs to wrestle with fundamental tensions across various desirable properties of prompt privacy. Thus, such continued attempts towards a unified framework need to be reconsidered. We recommend three critical paths forward: application-specific deployment of LLMs, context-specific evaluation of privacy frameworks, and better privacy literacy.

[640] arXiv:2610.29926 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Task-Preserving Multilingual Instruction Tuning for Open-Ended QA in WMT 2026 MIST
Aleix Sant, Jordi Luque, Carlos Escolano
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

This paper describes our submission to the WMT 2026 Multilingual Instruction Shared Task. We adapt Qwen3-8B with LoRA using organiser-provided data, EuroAlpaca, a multilingual instruction dataset created through task-preserving localisation, and CrossEuroAlpaca, a cross-lingual augmentation that assigns different source and target languages to instructions, contexts and responses. Our system targets open-ended question answering (QA-OEG) in ten shared-task languages represented in the auxiliary data. Under matched decoding, adaptation improves the mean Gemma-4 judge score on target-language QA-OEG by 7.8% relative to the base model. On an additional evaluation using the Aya Evaluation Suite across all shared-task languages, it yields relative gains of 41.5% in macro-averaged ROUGE-L and 2.9% in BERTScore-F1, with larger improvements in target languages. However, these gains are task- and language-specific. Gemma-4 scores improve for QA-OEG and summarisation in the target languages but decline for context-grounded QA there and across all three tasks in the non-target languages.

[641] arXiv:2610.29927 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Your Benchmark Is an Empirical Measure Over Difficulty
Yifan Sun, Naicheng Yu, Jiawen Gong, Jingyan Shen, Huan Zhang
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

A benchmark is not merely a collection of test questions; it naturally induces an empirical measure over difficulty. In this work, we develop this measure-based view of benchmark evaluation. This perspective allows us to identify and formalize two central failure modes: measure mismatch, where the benchmark difficulty distribution differs from the intended difficulty distribution, and coverage gaps, where uncovered regions along the difficulty axis prevent benchmarks from detecting meaningful localized training progress. We propose two diagnostic metrics that capture these two failure modes and provide rigorous theoretical guarantees. Empirically, we analyze 25 popular benchmarks spanning 7 domains using carefully estimated item difficulties. Our results show that many benchmarks implicitly overweight certain difficulty regions, so their leaderboard conclusions should be interpreted with caution; others leave substantial portions of the difficulty axis uncovered, limiting their ability to monitor the model improvement process. Finally, we turn diagnosis into action by introducing BenchFill, a simple difficulty-targeted item rewriting algorithm that effectively reduces local coverage gaps.

[642] arXiv:2610.29928 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Learned Musical-Time Coordinate for Piano Audio-to-Score Transcription
Min-Hsing Wang, Tsung-Ren Huang
Comments: 5 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ICASSP 2027
Subjects: Sound (cs.SD); Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS)

End-to-end piano audio-to-score (A2S) transcription is the task of reconstructing a notated score from an audio recording in a single system. Existing A2S approaches usually rely on pre-segmented excerpts, and few handle whole pieces without external segmentation. This raises the question of whether a musical-time coordinate can guide score transcription while also helping the system segment whole pieces. Previous work on jazz saxophone A2S uses an external beat tracker to obtain such a coordinate for score prediction. We introduce downbeat phase, a musical-time coordinate learned jointly with score transcription that represents each audio frame's relative position within a notated bar. With this coordinate, our system can not only condition its score decoder on downbeat phase but also self-segment at bar boundaries and stitch the segments into a whole piece. Evaluation suggests that the coordinate improves metrical structure and supports whole-piece transcription with comparable notation quality.

[643] arXiv:2610.29929 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Privacy Preference Controls for Agentic Systems
Shreya Kochar, Peeranat Sugsavanvit, Vidur Gupta, Joseph A. Calandrino, Deepak Kumar, Brett Frischmann, Sebastian Zimmeck
Comments: 27 pages, 4 figures, 7 tables
Subjects: Computers and Society (cs.CY); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

In response to vast and widespread online tracking, regulators and technologists alike have worked to develop laws and tools that allow people to express their privacy preferences. These measures seek to offer users greater control over the sale and sharing of personal information, putting agency in their hands to protect their privacy. However, the web is undergoing a seismic shift, away from strictly \textit{user-driven} behavior towards \textit{agentic behavior}, where AI agents take autonomous actions on behalf of users. In this study, we ask: What should privacy preference controls look like in the agentic web and agentic systems more generally? To answer this question, we develop a taxonomy of enforceable privacy preferences for agentic systems. Our taxonomy is informed both by laws and empirical studies of existing privacy tools as well as an audit of 30 leading AI assistants and agent platforms. To explore how our taxonomy can be implemented, we design and develop eight open-source prototypes that mirror real-world agentic applications and demonstrate how major aspects of our taxonomy can be structurally integrated in agentic protocols, such as the Model Control Protocol and Agent2Agent protocol. Ultimately, our study seeks to provide the groundwork for ensuring end-user privacy and autonomy is not lost in the newly arriving agentic world.

[644] arXiv:2610.29932 [pdf, html, other]
Title: FrontierCS 2: A Benchmark for Computer Science R&D
Qiuyang Mang, Wenhao Chai, Runyuan He, Dongruixuan Li, Zihan Zheng, Yujun He, Xuanyi Zhou, Hao Wang, Siddhant Ray, Bo Peng, Ruyi Ji, Shuo Yang, Haocheng Xi, Boru Chen, Xinyang David Han, Melissa Pan, Mayank Mishra, Boxi Yu, Sijia Liu, Kerem Akillioglu, Yi Pan, Zirui Wang, Mert Cemri, Diogo Antunes, Yichuan Wang, Aiwei Ivy Zhang, Zhenyang Chen, Qizheng Zhang, Kaiyuan Liu, Wenyuan Huang, Sherry Ruan, Shu Liu, Dacheng Li, Zerui Cheng, Zeyu Shen, Shang Zhou, Hanfei Chen, Yuzhong Zhang, Bohan Lyu, Qu Ao, Han Zheng, Chonghe Jiang, Jingzhuo Hu, Xiaokun Chen, Kunjun Li, Zhiqing Zhong, Haoye Tian, Tong Zhao, Yunzhong He, Hanchen Li, Ofir Press, Jiantao Jiao, Kunle Olukotun, Karthik R. Narasimhan, Jingbo Shang, Koushik Sen, Matei Zaharia, Alex Dimakis, Ion Stoica, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Alvin Cheung
Comments: Website: this https URL ; Code: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Can LLM agents make contributions to frontier computer science R&D? We introduce FrontierCS 2, a benchmark of 48 open-ended tasks. We take a paper and the code its authors released and delete the paper's contribution. The deleted code becomes the human reference that sets the bar. Earlier open-ended benchmarks give each agent a problem statement and grade one program after the run. FrontierCS 2 places the agent inside a research environment. The agent inherits a working repository and may submit a patch at any point. For each patch, a judge returns a development-suite score but keeps the evaluator, the held-out final suite and the reference private, and grades the final submission on that suite against the reference. The tasks span 13 domains, from machine-learning systems and high-performance computing to databases, security and robotics. Beyond these 48 tasks, FrontierCS 2 keeps a private set of more than 100 tasks, to be announced in the future. We evaluate 12 agents. The best one is Claude Opus 5.5, passing 58% of its runs. No run passes on 16 tasks. A higher score is not the same as a pass: most runs that beat the reference on the combined final score still fall short on some metric or workload. On a shared capability scale for agents and tasks, the median task is roughly as difficult as what the strongest agent can handle.

[645] arXiv:2610.29933 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Graph Topology Meets Energy-Driven Pathfinding: Preserving Contextual Consistency in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
Yufeng Li, Zaijing Li, Fuchen Zhang, Zongzong Wu, Ming Zhao, Fengxiao Tang
Comments: Accepted to Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2026
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) frequently integrates knowledge graphs (KGs) for complex multi-hop question answering. However, their performance is increasingly bottlenecked by the knowledge structuring and reasoning processes. (i) Severe semantic loss: Distilling continuous texts into discrete symbols strips away contextual nuances and narrative coherence. (ii) Pronounced modality mismatch: Fragmented graph structures clash with the continuous texts LLMs are pre-trained on, while rewriting them into natural language introduces generative noise and omits information. To address these limitations, we propose ThreadRAG, a semantic-topology-based RAG framework for context-preserving knowledge structuring and modality-native evidence reasoning. ThreadRAG introduces a Semantic Topology Mapper (STM), which organizes retrieved documents into context-intact Semantic Nodes and constructs a Semantic Topology Graph (STG) through narrative, semantic, and lexical edges. It further incorporates Energy-Driven Pathfinding (EDP), which identifies query-relevant subgraphs via energy diffusion and deterministically linearizes them into coherent textual evidence paths. Experiments on three multi-hop QA benchmarks demonstrate that ThreadRAG consistently outperforms strong baselines. Notably, it achieves a 14.4% EM improvement over text-centric methods on HotpotQA and surpasses the best baseline by 5.8% EM on 2WikiMultihop, while reducing token cost to 23.3% of the strongest baseline.

[646] arXiv:2610.29934 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ToM2Vec: Continuous Theory-of-Mind Tokens for Multi-Agent Coordination
Nithin Sivakumaran, Ali Payani, Hyunji Lee, Mohit Bansal, Elias Stengel-Eskin
Comments: Code: this https URL
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA)

Forming an accurate theory-of-mind (ToM) is key to successful multi-agent collaboration and requires reasoning under uncertainty to capture multiple possible partner states. This is hard to do in the text representation space native to large language model (LLM) agents, which more easily describe a single partner state. To address this challenge, we introduce ToM2Vec, which learns to form abstract theories-of-mind in a rich latent space via a fixed budget of continuous reasoning tokens. During training, supervision for these tokens comes from the partner's actual thoughts, which the ToM tokens are trained to abstract and match. At test-time, ToM tokens are generated by each agent and act as conditioners for that agent's thoughts and actions. Across several environments covering collaborative, competitive, and mixed-motive settings (Overcooked-AI, multiparty negotiation, Decrypto, Hanabi, and Collab Escape/Capture), we evaluate ToM2Vec's ability to support multi-agent interactions and collaboration, finding consistent improvements over the base model and a variety of competitive trained and prompted baselines. We show that latent reasoning is critical, with performance dropping when reasoning is expressed in text. Moreover, we show that ToM2Vec training generalizes to partner model families not seen at train-time, including a proprietary model (GPT-5.4). In our analysis, we provide evidence that the latent tokens encode a ToM, rather than task-specific information: ToM2Vec's tokens improve the agent's ability to directly answer questions about partner beliefs, desires, and next actions.

[647] arXiv:2610.29936 [pdf, html, other]
Title: DewHand: Direct Metric World-Space Hand Motion Reconstruction from Egocentric Videos
Naru Suzuki, Satoshi Ikehata, Takehiko Ohkawa, Yoichi Sato, Shuhei Kurita
Comments: Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Recovering metric world-space hand motion from egocentric video supports understanding human interactions and transferring them to embodied agents. Three challenges complicate this task: multi-stage pipelines propagate errors from independently estimated hand and camera motion; monocular observations leave physical scale ambiguous; and occlusion and out-of-view hands admit multiple plausible motion trajectories. We present DewHand, a unified model for direct joint reconstruction of world-space hand and camera motion. To avoid compounding errors from multi-stage estimation, DewHand jointly predicts hand and camera motion in a shared world coordinate system within a single-stage pipeline. To resolve metric-scale ambiguity, it combines scene-level geometric features from VGGT-$\Omega$ with metric-space supervision, while hand-specific features preserve fine-grained articulation. To handle occlusion and out-of-view hands, we formulate reconstruction as conditional motion generation with flow matching. Under the same architecture, this generative formulation outperforms direct regression in both accuracy and temporal smoothness with only two sampling steps. Experiments on HOT3D and ARCTIC demonstrate improved world-space accuracy and temporal consistency over state-of-the-art methods. DewHand reduces rigid-aligned world-space error relative to StableHand from 32.9 to 28.4 mm on HOT3D and from 76.2 to 36.2 mm on ARCTIC. It also recovers camera scale within 10% on two thirds of HOT3D clips, versus about a quarter for SLAM. Moreover, in zero-shot evaluations on HoloAssist, H2O, and TACO, captured with different devices, DewHand achieves the lowest rigid-aligned world-space error (WA-MPJPE) on each dataset.

[648] arXiv:2610.29939 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ERCLIP: Small-Data Adaptation of CLIP for Free-Length Image-Text Retrieval
Hoang-Bao Le, Allie Tran, Binh T. Nguyen, Liting Zhou, Cathal Gurrin
Comments: Accepted at LFSD - ACCV 2026 Worshop
Subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

CLIP's 77-token text encoder truncates detailed image descriptions. We present ERCLIP, a small-data adaptation of CLIP for long-caption image--text retrieval. During training, a long caption is split into sentences that the CLIP text encoder encodes independently; the sentence embeddings are fused by mean pooling or a gated residual Transformer scorer and receive their own contrastive loss. At inference ERCLIP is an unmodified CLIP dual encoder: test captions are still read through the 77-token window, and only training sees the full caption. We find that this fine-tuning erodes CLIP's zero-shot classification, most when the fusion output is not a combination of CLIP embeddings, and add a frozen-CLIP preservation loss on the image and short-caption embeddings. With 20k pairs and one epoch, ERCLIP improves long-caption R@1 over CLIP by 6.5--11.2 points, closing 62--77% of the gap to LongCLIP with 2% of its long captions. Preservation recovers 1.5--2.1 ImageNet zero-shot points (30--42% of the loss) and adds up to 2.4 points of COCO image-to-text R@1, at no inference cost.

[649] arXiv:2610.29943 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Towards English - Mizo Legal Machine Translation: Corpus Creation, Analysis, and Benchmarks
Telem Joyson Singh, Sanabam Boyshana, Sanasam Ranbir Singh, Priyankoo Sarmah
Comments: Accepted in OCOCOSDA 2026
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Indian court proceedings are held in English, so speakers of languages with limited translation technology have limited access to them. We present the first English Mizo parallel dataset of Indian court judgments. It contains 13,168 sentence pairs from the Gauhati High Court and the Supreme Court of India. Professional native Mizo translators translated complete documents; sentence pairs were manually aligned, and two independent reviewers checked the results. Our study finds that English words are borrowed in a very selective way: official and legal terms are almost always kept in English, but words for everyday things like actions, situations, and results are usually expressed in native Mizo. Mizo diacritics are also used inconsistently across the corpus. When we fine tune the NLLB 200 1.3B model on our training data, it scores 27.47 BLEU on a balanced legal test set of 1,000 sentence pairs, an improvement of 7.16 BLEU over the base model. However, it still uses English words about three times more often than a human translator does.

[650] arXiv:2610.29945 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Pre-emptive Carbon Aware Scheduling for Edge Workloads
Cecilia Chen, Rajni Dabas, Samir Khuller, Emilie Rivkin
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

Power grids use a constantly changing mix of fossil fuels and clean renewables like solar and wind. Because of this, the {\em carbon footprint} fluctuates drastically based on time and geographic location. Time-varying carbon intensity creates opportunities to reduce carbon emissions by shifting workloads to cleaner periods, but deadlines, task dependencies, and limited edge capacity constrain this flexibility. We study carbon-aware scheduling of jobs with release times, deadlines, and arbitrary precedence constraints under piecewise-constant carbon costs. Jobs execute preemptively on a single edge server or are outsourced at job-dependent costs to an unlimited-capacity cloud, modeled as providing instantaneous execution. The objective is to minimize the sum of edge carbon costs and cloud outsourcing costs while satisfying all timing and precedence constraints. For edge-only execution, we give an exact polynomial-time algorithm. Allowing cloud outsourcing makes the problem NP-hard, but we obtain a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme through a reduction to preemptive scheduling with rejection penalties (weighted tardiness). In contrast, even two edge servers without job migration admit no polynomially bounded approximation when carbon-cost variation is unrestricted, unless \(P=NP\). We complement these theoretical results with experiments on controlled synthetic workloads and production-derived Alibaba traces. On synthetic instances, our incremental max-flow implementation is $4.96\times$ faster on average than a direct min-cost flow, while experiements on production-derived workloads evaluate its performance under realistic job structures.

[651] arXiv:2610.29953 [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Plantwide Simulation Library for Control-Oriented Design: Analytical and Data-driven Use Cases
Kyle Territo, Luis A. Briceno-Mena, Jose A. Romagnoli
Comments: 6 pages, 3 figures, Submitted to the American Control Conference (ACC) 2027
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Control structures and operability indices for plantwide processes are developed and compared on fixed simulated flowsheets, and the configuration of a study is rarely reported in a form that another group can reproduce. In this contribution, plantbench, a library of plantwide process simulations in which the design, the controller tuning and the instrumentation of a plant are declared as hashed plain-data configurations, is presented. On a heat-integrated reactor--separator--recycle plant with an open-loop unstable reactor, a heuristic plantwide control design prices four heat-exchanger networks (HENs) by the least damping ratio of the linearized closed loop, and 2016 closed-loop runs over networks, tuning, analyzer deadtime and upsets test that ranking. Results show that the damping ratio orders the networks as the runs do with the network that recovers the most heat reaching 0.013 against 0.157 for the selected one and cycling under a throughput increase, but that it is a weak detector of which operation will oscillate. At the recall of a random forest on the first 100 min after an upset, 60 of 82 limit cycles, a damping-ratio threshold raises 173 false alarms against 5. The integral time of the temperature loop, to which the damping ratio is nearly insensitive, decides in part whether the plant holds an operating point.

[652] arXiv:2610.29954 [pdf, html, other]
Title: The Capacity of Interactive Secure Summation
Hua Sun
Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT)

In secure summation, $K$ parties each hold an input, and the sum of the inputs is computed at one party, securely against at most $T$ colluding parties. Communication typically takes one hop: each party sends one message directly to the party that computes the sum, using correlated randomness that is independent of the inputs and held in advance. We consider interactive secure summation, where every pair of parties is connected by a secure link, so that each party can send messages to every other party, each party has only independent local randomness, and the messages may depend on the inputs and on earlier messages over multiple rounds. We characterize the capacity region, the set of achievable rates of communication, counting all messages exchanged among the parties over all rounds, and of the randomness of every party, counted in symbols per symbol of the sum. For $0\le T\le K-2$, the optimal communication rate is $K(K-1)/(K-T)$, and the randomness rates form a polyhedron with, up to a relabeling of the parties, a single extreme point: $T$ parties have the randomness rates $(K+T-2t)/(K-T)$, $t=1,\ldots,T$, and the others none. In particular, the optimal total randomness rate is $T(K-1)/(K-T)$. Linear schemes achieve every extreme point together with the optimal communication rate. The same techniques give the capacity region when every party recovers the sum and when the sum is computed at a server without input.

[653] arXiv:2610.29959 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Training-free Acceleration for Blind Compressed Image Restoration via Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition
Suhang Yao, Xin Li, Xijun Wang, Yufei Wang, Yeying Jin, Zhibo Chen
Comments: 12 pages. Accepted for publication in IEEE Journal on Emerging and Selected Topics in Circuits and Systems
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Transformer-based models achieve strong performance on blind compressed image restoration (CIR) under unknown compression settings, but their densely stacked projection operators make deployment costly. We study training-free acceleration for such models through an empirical, operator-level analysis. Specifically, we profile where computation is concentrated, characterize channel-wise activation distributions under compressed inputs, and examine the singular-value decay of representative projection weights. These measurements identify the recurring projections in the attention, feed-forward, convolutional, and prompt-conditioning pathways as effective low-rank replacement targets that preserve the original inference graph. They further establish truncated SVD (TSVD) as a principled training-free baseline for blind CIR and reveal why a uniform low-rank objective is mismatched to the channel-imbalanced feature distributions of compressed images. Accordingly, we formulate Activation-Calibrated Singular Value Decomposition (ASVD) for this restoration setting, deriving low-rank factors entirely offline from pretrained weights and lightweight activation statistics gathered from only a few compressed calibration images. By weighting the decomposition with channel-wise activation magnitudes, our ASVD assigns larger penalties to errors on more active channels, requiring neither retraining nor online calibration and leaving the restoration pipeline intact. When instantiated on PromptCIR at rank 64, ASVD consistently improves PSNR-B over TSVD across four standard benchmarks under identical parameter and MAC budgets. At this operating point, the factorized model cuts parameters by 59% (34.75M to 14.34M) and computation by 16.1% (258.79 to 217.16 GMACs for a 256 x 256 input), enabling acceleration without retraining.

[654] arXiv:2610.29961 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Commit or Abstain? System One Decision Models, LLMs, and Missing Legal Authority
M. Mikail Demir
Comments: 16 pages, 4 figures, 4 tables. Under review. Code, data, and model outputs: this https URL
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Given the enormous number of claims to be checked, verifiable legal AI requires scalable, cost-effective models that answer the practical needs of law. System One decision models are built on large language models but, instead of generating text, return a calibrated probability for each option. This suits the verification of legal authority, where the question is closed: a given holding, or none of them. We test whether such models abstain when the correct authority is missing. We extend CaseHOLD with an abstention condition in which the correct holding is replaced in 1,670 of 5,314 items, and compare four decision models with six generative LLMs. When no option is correct, generative LLMs still pick one in 38-86% of items; the most cautious decision model does so in 30%. On standard CaseHOLD, a decision model matches the best generative LLM (88.1% vs. 88.2%) at 1/55 of the cost. Accepting that LLM's answer only when a decision model agrees halves its wrong citations, and distilling a decision model's probabilities into Qwen3-8B, without labels, yields a well-calibrated local model. Legal AI should be judged by its wrong citations, not by accuracy alone.

[655] arXiv:2610.29964 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Object- and Task-Aware Active Perception for Safe Navigation of Mobile Manipulators in Semi-Static Environments
Jingxing Qian, Xintong Du, Jun Yang, Siqi Zhou, Steven L. Waslander, Angela P. Schoellig
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Mobile manipulators must navigate safely in cluttered, partially unknown environments across logistics, manufacturing, and service applications. Semi-static changes between robot visits can lead to outdated scene knowledge and increased collision risk. We propose an active perception framework that enables a high degree-of-freedom (DoF) mobile manipulator to inspect uncertain or safety-critical regions with its hand camera during navigation. A probabilistic, object- and task-aware next-best-view (NBV) formulation prioritizes observations near the desired path and around uncertain or potentially changing objects. The perception objective is integrated into hierarchical-task model predictive control (HTMPC), exploiting kinematic redundancy for viewpoint adjustment while preserving the higher priority of base-trajectory tracking. The system unifies navigation, map maintenance, and active perception in a closed loop. Real-world tests show improved map consistency, reduced task-dependent map entropy, and lower navigation risk than passive or non-task-aware baselines. Additional simulation and real-world sequences demonstrate responses to controlled semi-static scene changes.

[656] arXiv:2610.29965 [pdf, html, other]
Title: CORD: Conflict-Aware Optimization for Joint RL and Distillation in Agents
Wenhao Yu, Zhengcheng Wang, Jiahong Liu, Zexuan Qiu, Minda Hu, Shaohang Wei, Jiafei Lyu, Junyan Lyu, Haobo Fu, Irwin King
Comments: 38 pages, 12 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Joint reinforcement learning and self-distillation combines task rewards with dense teacher guidance for agent training, but their gradients can partly cancel. A mixing coefficient controls relative scale without selectively removing opposing components. We present CORD, a general framework for conflict-aware optimization of two objectives. CORD separates the choice of protected objective from the condition that triggers projection, and combines the gradients once per optimizer mini-batch. A nearest-point formulation yields a closed-form update and characterizes its first-order effect on the protected objective before optimizer transformations. Gradient diagnostics connect conflict in agent training to lost local optimization progress and motivate selective correction. As a gradient-combination mechanism, CORD can be added to different joint training recipes while retaining their objectives. Across three such recipes, it improves ALFWorld success by 1.5-15.9 percentage points. On WebShop, it improves two of the three pairs, with SDAR rising from 60.7% to 64.6% success. Our analyses explain why protection direction and projection gate must be chosen together, and why the distillation objective and its mixing weight remain consequential after projection.

[657] arXiv:2610.29968 [pdf, other]
Title: CulturalRiddles: A Multicultural Benchmark of Riddles
My Chiffon Nguyen, Tianyi Hu, Vinod Anbalagan, Henry Gagnier, Pouya Sadeghi, Farah Abdou, Tidor-Vlad Pricope, Diego MMS Oliveira, Jocelyn K D'Arcy, Madeline Smith, Oluwaseun A Ajayi, Yusser Al Ghussin, Zena Al-Khalili, Micol Altomare, Shayan Amir, Ahanaf Aziz, Bryan Chen, Ruchira Dhar, Abdellah El Mekki, Rawan Mohammed Elframawy, Akhil Eppa, Silvia Fernandez, Alex Gimei, Arya Hariharan, Christian Hoang, RamMohanRao Kadiyala, Diana Kozachek, Peerat Limkonchotiwat, Ankita Maity, Di Mo, Ayush Munot, Aylin Naebzadeh, Anastasiia Nikitina, Dina Pisarevskaya, Divas Poudel, Jebish Purbey, Md Rabius Sany Apu, Ahmad Mufli Ramadhan, Ralitza Nikolova Rizova, Diogo M. Serrano-Miranda, Vivek Gopalkrishna Silimkhan, Luis Fernando Solis Navarro, Kaiser Sun, Arya Suneesh, Manaswitha Sunkara, Tejaswi Sunkara, Jonathan E Swindell, Hanna Yukhymenko, Jingyi Zheng, Esther Adenuga, Ilia Afanasev, Wafa Aissa, Lisa Alazraki, Lauren C Altomare, Priscilla Amondi Amuok, Emile Anand, Gabriel Assis, José Matías Avalos, Silvia Lorena Avila, Zakaria Baannou, Niyati Bafna, Yash Bagla, Sarah Bahrami, Bontu F Balcha, Vanya Bannihatti Kumar, Irene Baucells, Abdumutalib Begmuratov, Naman Bhatia, Souvik Bhattacharyya, Isabel Blanco Ferreiro, Felipe Bochini, Sayuru Bopitiya, Angana Borah, Tulika Bose, Olena Bugaiova, Juliana Carvalho, Nancy F Chen, Stephy Chen, Rochelle Choenni, Jayanth Krishna Chundru, Leandro A Cossio, Nebojša Damnjanović, Ona de Gibert, Marco De Santis, Pedro Delgado, Kaustubh Dholé, Adnan El Assadi, Wesam El-Sayed, Nadine M Elframawy, Oumayma Essarhi, Naome A Etori, Reuben Chagas Fernandes, Saanidhi Pravin Gade, Javier García Gilabert, Álvaro González-Escapa, Bin Hu, Kaiyu Huang, Abderrahmane Issam, Danka Jokić, Ulugbek Khalilov
Comments: 37 pages. Dataset: this https URL Code: this https URL
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

As LLMs expand their language coverage, evaluating how well they understand and represent diverse cultures becomes increasingly important. However, many benchmarks remain English-centric, with limited cultural coverage and a focus on factual knowledge over its application in real-world cultural contexts. We propose CulturalRiddles, a benchmark of original, culturally grounded riddles created entirely by humans through a participatory community effort, spanning 62 cultures (45 countries, 51 languages). These riddles are deeply rooted in their respective cultures and require abductive and compositional reasoning, alongside detailed factual and social knowledge, language skills, and an understanding of culturally specific associations. We benchmark 28 LLM configurations using both automatic and large-scale human evaluation. Even frontier models achieve at most 22% accuracy in some communities. We publicly release all artifacts alongside an open contribution process to expand the benchmark's linguistic and cultural coverage.

[658] arXiv:2610.29969 [pdf, html, other]
Title: FaultGene: LLM-Assisted Fault-Augmented Test Generation for Hardware-in-the-Loop Validation of Autonomous Driving Systems
Chaoran Yuan, Fadi Kurdahi
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Reliable validation of autonomous driving cyber-physical systems requires testing not only nominal driving behavior but also failures arising from faults in sensing and embedded computation. Physical road testing provides realistic system behavior but is costly and difficult to reproduce, while simulation enables scalable evaluation but cannot fully capture hardware-dependent behavior and fault propagation. Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) validation bridges this gap by executing the driving stack on real embedded hardware within a simulated environment. However, preparing fault-augmented scenarios for HIL testing remains largely a manual process, limiting test coverage, scalability, and efficiency.
We present FaultGene, an LLM-assisted framework for automated generation of executable fault-augmented tests for HIL fault-resilience validation. Given a baseline Scenic/CARLA scenario and a structured fault specification, FaultGene generates a fault-augmented test case that captures the effects of HIL-level fault injection. During offline refinement, semantic-consistency checks and execution-level feedback are used to correct candidates that fail to preserve the intended scenario context or produce the desired fault-induced degradation, and to construct high-quality supervision for fine-tuning. The resulting generator then produces fault-augmented tests directly at deployment time without requiring manually engineered reference executions or repeated refinement loops.

[659] arXiv:2610.29983 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Free-XOR TFHE via Lazy Bootstrapping
Ali Ajorian, Osman Biçer
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Gate bootstrapping (GB) is a widely used technique in FHEW-like fully homomorphic encryption schemes, such as TFHE, for evaluating Boolean gates while simultaneously reducing the noise of the resulting ciphertext. However, the computational cost of GB is typically dominated by an expensive blind rotation (BR). \cite{chen2024free} proposed a gate bootstrapping framework in which $\txor$ gates can be evaluated simply by adding the two input ciphertexts, resulting in what they call \textit{free-XOR}. To obtain a functionally complete set of operations, they further designed a GB procedure for evaluating $\tand$ gates using two lightweight blind rotations. In this work, we propose a similar gate bootstrapping framework that supports free evaluation of $\txor$ gates while evaluating \textit{all symmetric binary Boolean gates}, i.e., the 8 gates whose output is identical for the inputs $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$, using two blind rotations. In addition to providing broader gate support, our construction is substantially simpler than that of \cite{chen2024free}, both conceptually and in terms of implementation.

[660] arXiv:2610.29984 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Constrained Koopman Control Parametrization: Convex Controller Synthesis for Tracking under Input Constraints
Taha Ondogan, Ran Jing, Andrew P. Sabelhaus, Roberto Tron
Comments: 16 pages, 8 figures
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Koopman operator theory represents nonlinear systems with linear and bilinear terms in the state and input observables, greatly simplifying control design. However, incorporating input constraints into Koopman-based controller synthesis remains challenging, limiting their applicability to constrained control tasks such as tracking. This paper develops a constrained Koopman Control Parametrization (cKoCoP) framework for synthesizing state-feedback controllers that satisfy prescribed input constraints with Lyapunov-certified stability of the identified lifted closed loop. The cKoCoP offers nonlinear state-feedback via linear-in-observables feedback, enabling linear controller design. The proposed controller is obtained through convex optimization: we incorporate ellipsoidal or polytopic input constraints with the S-procedure or Farkas-lemma-based conditions. We also introduce a Control Lyapunov Function (CLF) for trajectory tracking which incorporates input constraints. The approach is validated on two canonical nonlinear systems, a double pendulum and a unicycle, demonstrating data-driven tracking while respecting input constraints. Experiments validate the method's robustness to measurement noise, and runtime improvements over Koopman Model Predictive Control (KMPC) baselines. The results demonstrate that cKoCoP achieves competitive tracking performance with substantially reduced online computational cost, supporting its potential for real-time constrained tracking applications.

[661] arXiv:2610.29985 [pdf, html, other]
Title: TIDE: Tree-Induced Fine-Grained Diagnostic Evaluation from Model Behaviors
Jiayi Chen, Hui Li, Yujiong Shen, Qiyuan Peng, Yanxin Li, Chenhao Huang, Shaofan Liu, Guoqiang Zhang, Junjie Ye, Shihan Dou, Ming Zhang, Maxm Pan, Tao Gui, Qi Zhang, Xuanjing Huang
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Benchmark performance is the dominant standard for comparing large language models (LLMs), typically summarized by a single aggregate score, such as accuracy, pass rate, or rubric score. This aggregate score provides limited information about a model's underlying capabilities, yet understanding these capabilities is crucial for model development and evaluation. To this end, we propose Tree-Induced Diagnostic Evaluation (TIDE), which recasts diagnostic evaluation as behavior-driven decision-tree induction to perform fine-grained capability diagnosis. TIDE recursively builds a hierarchical capability tree from benchmark samples and model scores: at each node, an LLM judge proposes candidate splits and performs sample-to-group classification, and behavior-based information gain selects among them. We apply TIDE to five models across four benchmarks to demonstrate its effectiveness, and find fine-grained capability contrasts invisible at the aggregate level: Claude Opus 4.6 achieves 100% on microeconomic market reasoning where GPT-5.4 scores 83.3%, but trails GPT-5.4 on contract law reasoning with 77.8% versus 88.9%. We hope TIDE can be extended to past and future benchmarks so that the rich behavioral signal in evaluation results is fully leveraged for understanding model capabilities.

[662] arXiv:2610.29987 [pdf, html, other]
Title: GhostFaceMPC: Privacy-Preserving Face Recognition with Multi-Party Computation
Davide Carnemolla, Dario Catalano, Mario Di Raimondo
Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR)

Facial recognition has become central to modern authentication systems, security frameworks, and personalized services. However, its widespread adoption is hindered by severe privacy risks, particularly surrounding unauthorized access to sensitive biometric data. To address these challenges, this paper presents GhostFaceMPC, the first end-to-end, privacy-preserving face recognition system to evaluate a deep convolutional neural network extractor and matching under secure multi-party computation. GhostFaceMPC enables secure processing of facial data across all stages of a face recognition process, from feature extraction and storage to matching, without exposing raw images or biometric embeddings at any stage. We introduce a multi-party computation-friendly quantization of the GhostFaceNet model and circuit optimizations that make face recognition under multi-party computation practical. The code is available at this https URL.

[663] arXiv:2610.29988 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Enumeration-based Triangle Counting on GPUs
Sayan Ghosh
Comments: 11 pages
Subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)

Subgraph enumeration in partitioned graphs across distributed-memory systems is beset with challenges in balancing data movement with the local computation. Especially, counting the number of triangles induced by the closed wedges (i.e., length-3 cycles) is a measure of connectedness in a graph, but often limited by the significant search space caused by open wedges or length-2 paths (usually greater than the number of edges in a graph), which must be inspected to assess whether a particular wedge is closed. To mitigate triangle counting on massive graphs, distributed-memory partitioned-graph approaches are viable (i.e., assessing closed wedges independently within a partition), but load imbalance due to arbitrary communication can overshadow any gains from enhanced concurrency, owing to the inherent lack of structure in regular graphs.
In this paper, we discuss a distributed-memory exact graph triangle counting implementation, and assess its performance over billion-edge real-world graphs on contemporary scale-out and scale-up based NVIDIA GPU platforms (considering NVIDIA ``Ampere'' and ``Hopper'' architectures), depicting a scalability spectrum of multiple orders of magnitude. Comparisons with existing state-of-the-art approaches demonstrates up to 10$\times$ improvements relative to distributed-memory CPU baseline, 2-100$\times$ over single-GPU vendor-optimized NVIDIA RAPIDS cuGraph and 10-60\% over multi-GPU $G^2$Miner, in terms of end-to-end execution times.

[664] arXiv:2610.29989 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Looking Ahead: Modeling Future Evolution in Autoregressive Video Generation
Ruopeng Gao, Yukun Huang, Jiarui Hu, Shuai Wang, Wenbo Hu, Ying Shan, Limin Wang
Comments: Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Autoregressive video diffusion models generate videos chunk by chunk, yet producing plausible continuations does not guarantee that they capture how scenes evolve. Under teacher forcing, strong temporal redundancy may allow local visual continuity to serve as a shortcut for current-chunk denoising, reducing the pressure to model visual evolution. We introduce Future Chunk Prediction (FCP), an auxiliary objective jointly optimized with teacher-forced denoising that predicts temporally separated chunks without access to the intervening visual context. Drawing supervision directly from training videos, FCP requires no additional pretrained visual encoder and leaves autoregressive inference unchanged. Our method achieves superior physical plausibility over standard teacher-forced autoregressive training with a lower overall training compute budget, highlighting the effectiveness and efficiency of future-chunk supervision for modeling visual evolution. Intriguingly, our visualizations suggest that FCP fosters a more structured representation space, which may be valuable for building autoregressive world models.

[665] arXiv:2610.29992 [pdf, html, other]
Title: SCDM: Scalable Causal Discovery in Nonlinear Temporal Systems with Meta-Learning
Jingbo Wang, Kegeng Tang, Zihao Wang, Shaogang Ren
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 44 pages, 6 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Causal discovery from nonlinear multivariate time series is challenging in high-dimensional systems, where the number of candidate directed relations grows quadratically with the number of variables. Existing methods are often limited by target-wise model fitting, repeated conditional testing, or expensive graph-search procedures. We propose SCDM, a shared-parameter meta-learning framework for scalable temporal causal discovery. SCDM treats each target variable as a task while learning a shared temporal predictor and a shared causal-strength matrix across tasks. Each meta-episode updates only a subset of target-variable tasks, allowing the model to accumulate structural evidence across the full system without exhaustive target-wise optimization. After training, a post-training graph readout converts the learned predictor into continuous directed causal scores for threshold-independent evaluation. We also provide a finite-error recovery principle showing that, under fully observed delayed-system assumptions and a positive risk-gap condition, thresholding SCDM scores recovers the graph when statistical, meta-optimization, and readout errors are below the population margin. Experiments on controlled synthetic, neuroimaging-inspired, high-dimensional, and real-world temporal benchmarks demonstrate competitive causal recovery and improved scalability in large temporal systems.

[666] arXiv:2610.29994 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Pinch-Free Orientations of Polyomino Grid Graphs
James Fox, Mirela Damian
Comments: 12 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Computational Geometry (cs.CG)

We study lattice-based collective construction of a target polyomino on the integer grid, where robots place unit square blocks subject to two physical constraints: the partial structure must remain connected at all times, and no placement may create an unfillable one-cell gap. We present a wavefront sweep algorithm that computes a dependency structure satisfying the local conditions required for safe assembly. Given a list of n cells sorted lexicographically by coordinates, the orientation can be computed in O(n) time using O(n) auxiliary space.

[667] arXiv:2610.29995 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Remembering Through Change: Provenance-Preserving Hypergraph Memory for Multimodal Agents
Jielong Tang, Ling-An Zeng, Xujie Yuan, Xiao Dong, Zhiqian Xia, Qingfeng Li, Shixiong Kai, Kaichao Liang, Rong Yao, Jian Yin
Comments: 31 pages,10 figures
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Long-term memory for multimodal agents remains challenging, as it must preserve fine-grained visual evidence while tracking entity evolution across sessions. Existing abstraction-based memories compress images into text, often discarding visually discriminative details, whereas pixel-preserving memories retain raw observations but struggle to reliably associate diverse observations with persistent entity identities and track their evolving states. To address these limitations, we propose MHG-Mem, a multimodal hypergraph memory that jointly organizes entity identity, state evolution, and provenance to visual evidence. Specifically, MHG-Mem represents distinct entity mentions and their observed facts as individual nodes, grouping identity-consistent mentions and facts through occurrence hyperedges. It then synthesizes aspect-specific evolution states from these grouped observations and links them to supporting entities, facts, and source evidence through evolutionary and evidential hyperedges. To navigate this structured memory, we introduce hypergraph-based agentic search, which adaptively selects an entry layer, traverses typed hyperedges across memory levels, and inspects source observations when fine-grained verification is required. These designs support both detailed visual verification and reasoning over cross-session state changes. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of MHG-Mem, improving performance by 8.20-9.98% over the strongest baseline.

[668] arXiv:2610.29996 [pdf, other]
Title: HiddenLens: A Multi-Layer LLM Framework for Detecting and Resolving Hidden Assumptions in Software Requirements
Tanu Singh, Aashna Suman, Vinod Patidar
Comments: 24 pages, 14 figures, 10 tables
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Natural-language software requirements often omit assumptions about performance, operating conditions, user behaviour, and domain constraints, affecting architecture, testing, and deployment. If undiscovered until implementation, resolving them is far more costly than addressing them early. Although ambiguity and vagueness are widely studied, less attention has been given to assumptions embedded in requirements that appear clear and reasonable. We propose HiddenLens, a novel six-layer BERT-LLM pipeline and, to our knowledge, the first framework engineered to detect, classify, question, and resolve hidden assumptions rather than merely flag ambiguity. Layer 1 uses BERT attention entropy to localise unresolved spans; Layer 2 uses CoT-prompted LLM reasoning to articulate each assumption and its failure risk; Layer 3 uses fine-tuned BERT to classify assumptions into six non-functional requirement categories: performance, security, scalability, usability, reliability, and domain; Layer 4 generates ranked clarification options using FS LLM prompting; Layer 5 enables human validation through confirmation, editing, or rephrasing; and Layer 6 rewrites the requirement using the confirmed resolution, producing an explicit, testable, and traceable requirement. We also introduce the HiddenLens Corpus (HLC), comprising 312 requirements annotated with 847 hidden assumptions across six NFR categories. Inspired by PROMISE and PURE, HLC addresses the lack of annotated data for this task and is, to our knowledge, the first dataset developed specifically for it. HiddenLens outperforms keyword-based and QuARS-Adapted baselines by 71% and 61%, respectively, achieving an end-to-end F1-score of 0.79; its BERT-based NFR classifier achieves an F1-score of 0.847. These results indicate that HiddenLens can help analysts resolve hidden assumptions before they propagate through software development.

[669] arXiv:2610.29997 [pdf, html, other]
Title: DONIC: Generalist Dexterous Bimanual Tracking Control from Human Demonstrations
Mingze Sun, Ziang Cao, Yuan Fei, Qiankuan Tao, Zihan Wang, Tianqi Liu, Junhao Chen, Haiwen Diao, Fangzhou Hong, Zhaoxi Chen, Ziwei Liu
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Despite recent progress in dexterous reference tracking, existing models focus primarily on single-hand manipulation and a limited range of interactions, leaving the bimanual dexterous behaviors common in real life unaddressed. The scarcity of contact-rich bimanual manipulation data and the increased complexity of coordinating contacts make developing a generalist bimanual tracker particularly challenging. Therefore, we present 1) DONIC, the first generalist bimanual tracker jointly trained across operation categories and human-motion sources, together with 2) BiHOI, a multi-view dataset of 1,575 sequences spanning 229 objects and emphasizing sustained bimanual interaction, where reconstructed interactions are retargeted into robot references. DONIC combines proximal policy optimization with behavioral cloning in a feedback loop that recycles verified successful executions into training demonstrations. An object-centered per-hand reward maintains object-motion feedback while supervising each hand according to its reference contact role. Clip-Centered Advantages remove reference-dependent advantage offsets while preserving within-trajectory differences. Together, these designs enable one single policy to learn coordinated manipulation across heterogeneous references. Without finetuning, a single checkpoint achieves 86.79% success on unseen trajectories of training objects and 57.32% on held-out objects, surpassing the state-of-the-art bimanual tracking baselines by 77.36 and 45.73 percentage points.

[670] arXiv:2610.29999 [pdf, html, other]
Title: EPIC: Rethinking Trust Regions for Autoregressive LLM Policies via Exact-KL Prefix Importance-Ratio Clipping
Chengxi Li, Hanlin Wu, Zhicheng Cai, Huan-ang Gao, Wei-Ying Ma, Jingjing Liu, Hao Zhou
Comments: 27 pages. Code: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Reinforcement learning (RL) based on PPO-style clipping has become an effective approach to improving the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, standard token-level clipping measures policy change only through the conditional probability of the current token, while the prefix conditioning context is itself generated by the policy. This mismatch becomes especially consequential in long-response and off-policy training. We reformulate autoregressive generation as a finite-horizon Markov decision process and derive its performance-difference identity under behavior-policy sampling. The resulting change of measure identifies the cumulative likelihood ratio of the generated prefix as the exact importance weight for each stepwise policy-improvement term. Starting from the monotonic-improvement principle of trust-region policy optimization, we then construct a prefix-level trust region using the exact reverse-KL coordinate $r-1-\log r$, whose behavior-policy expectation equals the corresponding prefix-distribution KL divergence. This yields EPIC, a PPO-style sequence-clipping method that directly regulates prefix-level policy drift without relying on a local quadratic approximation or expert-routing replay. Experiments on off-policy reinforcement learning with a sparse mixture-of-experts language model show that EPIC consistently outperforms standard and sequence-level clipping baselines across mathematical-reasoning benchmarks, while remaining competitive with routing-replay-based alternatives. Code is available at this https URL.

[671] arXiv:2610.30001 [pdf, html, other]
Title: When Majority-Vote Fails: Sequence Reconstruction under Fixed-Weight Substitutions
Vivian Papadopoulou, Yonatan Yehezkeally, V. Arvind Rameshwar, Antonia Wachter-Zeh
Subjects: Information Theory (cs.IT)

We consider the problem of binary sequence reconstruction where a sequence is transmitted multiple times over a channel, and each undergoes substitution errors by an arbitrary error vector of Hamming weight exactly $t$. We determine $N_{\mathrm{wc}}$, the minimum number of distinct channel output observations guaranteeing unique reconstruction by an optimal decoder, and show that the bit-wise majority-vote decoder, which was proved by Levenshtein (2001) to be optimal for channels corrupting up to $t$ bits, is in fact suboptimal here. Despite this suboptimality, we prove a condition that admits a practical early-termination rule, necessary for every decoder at any number of outputs $N$, and sufficient for bit-wise majority-vote even below $N_{\mathrm{wc}}$. We evaluate the number of outputs at which this condition is triggered, numerically, and show that it frequently occurs below $N_{\mathrm{wc}}$ when the block-length $k>2t+1$. Finally, we propose an alternative algorithm aimed at guaranteeing unique reconstruction with fewer observations than bit-wise majority-vote, and demonstrate through exhaustive enumeration that it successfully decodes channel output-sets where bit-wise majority-vote fails.

[672] arXiv:2610.30004 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Every Alarm Has a Cause: An Open Generator of Telecom Alarm Storms with Exact Root Causes, Bound to NORIA-O, RFC 8632 and TMF642
Madhulatha Mandarapu, Sandeep Kunkunuru
Comments: 22 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables. Generator: this https URL (Apache-2.0). The dataset deposit is prepared but not yet published, so this version cites no DOI; a revision will carry it
Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Alarm root-cause analysis is studied on data that cannot be shared. Operator logs are confidential, so what the field publishes is a causal graph between alarm types rather than per-incident causes, a fixed scenario set, gated, or never released. Two recent benchmarks carry per-incident root causes at scale; neither states a download location or a licence.
We give a generator rather than a dataset. It runs on real backbone topologies from the Internet Topology Zoo and records the exact root cause and the propagation path of every alarm -- a by-product of generation, not a labelling pass. Every emitted field binds to a term in NORIA-O, RFC 8632, RFC 8345 or TMF642, and an unknown term fails the run. We ship fixed configurations, splits, a scorer and nine baselines.
A one-line rule -- rank the device that raised the earliest critical alarm -- takes top-1 at 0.650 against 0.575 for our own temporal method, and wins 13 of 15 runs over three backbones and five seeds. An LLM given the same view reaches 0.600, the same model allowed to query the graph 0.625, and the rule wins on real operator alarms too, at 0.773: a property of alarm streams, not of our generator. One fault class separates the table: when a site loses power its PoP reports nothing, so every method that ranks alarmed devices scores 0.000 or near it, while the two that walk the topology to a silent candidate take 1.000 and 0.833.

[673] arXiv:2610.30006 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Building Auditable AI Text Detectors with Sparse Autoencoders
Liam Dugan, Callum McDougall, Matthew Denton, Philip Pham, Christine Kaeser-Chen, Chris Callison-Burch
Comments: EMNLP 2026
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

AI-generated text detectors are increasingly deployed in consequential settings---peer review, education, admissions, journalism, and content moderation---where their outputs directly affect individuals. Yet the strongest detectors are fine-tuned neural classifiers whose decisions are opaque, while transparent alternatives (stylometric and linguistic-feature classifiers) underperform them by wide margins. We present a pipeline that converts a fine-tuned neural detector into a classifier that operates on human-readable concepts. We accomplish this by training sparse autoencoders (SAEs) directly on a detector's residual stream, assigning auto-interpretation labels to each SAE feature, and retaining only features whose generated descriptions pass a global fidelity threshold. We then train a lightweight classifier on just the interpretable features. We find that our SAEs recover latent concepts that correspond to highly specific and predictive linguistic "tells" of AI-generated text. Classifiers built on these extracted features are not only highly interpretable but exhibit stronger performance on out-of-distribution texts than either neural or stylometric alternatives.

[674] arXiv:2610.30007 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Multiclass Boundary Refinement with Neural Cellular Automata for Remote Sensing Land Cover Segmentation
Pascoassis Souza Santos Meira, Gilson Antonio Giraldi, Rafael Duarte Coelho dos Santos
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Semantic segmentation of remote sensing imagery often places class boundaries a few pixels away from where they truly lie, and this position error is concentrated in the thin band measured by Boundary IoU (BIoU). We treat boundary refinement as the iterated application of a small learned local rule: the Boundary Refinement Neural Cellular Automaton (BRNCA), that starts from the class probabilities of a frozen, pre-trained segmenter and corrects them cell by cell. We generalise the binary rNCA to the multiclass case by keeping the visible channels on the probability simplex through an Aitchison (log-space) update and by adding free hidden channels. The best configuration improves the mean BIoU over the base segmenter by 2.36 points (from 46.63 to 48.99). The gain is concentrated on the irregular woodland class (+8.5 points BIoU); this suggests that position error is correlated with the fractal dimension of the class boundaries.

[675] arXiv:2610.30009 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Mitigating Model Collapse through Dreaming Learning
Matteo Benati, Alessandro Londei, Denise Lanzieri, Raffaello Mastromarino, Vittorio Loreto
Comments: 8 pages, 6 figures. Accepted at the 2nd Workshop on Principles of Generative Modeling (PriGM), NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Disordered Systems and Neural Networks (cond-mat.dis-nn); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Training generative models on synthetic data causes loss of diversity and a decrease in performance, a phenomenon known as model collapse. We study this degeneration spectrally in a controlled Markov setting. The eigenvalue spectrum of the learned transition operator offers a direct view of the process, since the subdominant eigenvalues set how fast the chain mixes and therefore how much of the state space it continues to explore. We find that sampling at temperature $T_s < 1$ acts on the operator like repeated sharpening, pushing it toward a deterministic system: the subdominant eigenvalues approach the unit circle and the spectral gap narrows. When $T_s < 1$, even data accumulation does not appear to arrest this drift. We then analyze Dreaming Learning, a regulariser that, in parallel with regular training, adds a loss term on the model's own samples drawn at a raised temperature $T_d > 1$. Because high-temperature samples flatten the predicted distribution, training on them keeps the entries of the learned operator from becoming vanishingly small, which in turn keeps the eigenvalues bounded away from the unit circle. Measurements of the spectra over 5000 generations are consistent with this picture, and the mitigation effect persists in more complex settings such as LSTM language models and a 124M-parameter GPT-2.

[676] arXiv:2610.30011 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Seeking Cost--Effective Incentive for Merchant MTDC Investment in an AC Grid: A Parametric MISOCP Model to VSC Siting and Sizing
Haixiao Li, Jure Lokar, Leopold Herman, Aleksandra Lekić
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Deploying voltage source converter (VSC)-based multi-terminal DC (MTDC) networks in existing AC grids offers a promising solution for alleviating transmission congestion, enhancing power-transfer capability, and improving operational economy. However, constructing an MTDC network requires participation from merchant investors. Therefore, the transmission system operator (TSO) responsible for the AC grid must provide an adequate economic incentive that enables merchant investors not only to recover the MTDC investment cost but also to earn a reasonable return commensurate with their risk and expectations. An insufficient incentive may fail to attract merchant investment, whereas an excessive incentive may unnecessarily reduce the economic benefits retained by the TSO. Determining an appropriate incentive that balances these competing interests therefore becomes a critical issue. To address this issue, this paper formulates a sharing-rate-parameterized mixed-integer second-order cone programming (MISOCP) model that jointly optimizes VSC siting and sizing while coordinating AC/DC system operation. A straightforward search procedure is then employed to identify the benefit-sharing rate that meets the investor's expectations while preserving sufficient benefits for the TSO. Case studies demonstrate the operating-cost benefits of MTDC integration and validate the proposed search strategy for seeking such a benefit-sharing rate.

[677] arXiv:2610.30013 [pdf, html, other]
Title: ClunoGS: Compact Language 3D Gaussian Splatting via Unified Optimization
Jian Xu, Yi Li, Ying Huang, Siyi Wu, Bingzhe Li, Yuede Ji, Miao Yin
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Language 3D Gaussian Splatting enables open-vocabulary scene understanding by associating Gaussian primitives with language features. These semantic attributes increase model storage, while most existing 3DGS compression methods are designed mainly to preserve RGB rendering quality. One straightforward approach is to apply sparsification and quantization sequentially. However, pruning based only on rendering quality can remove Gaussians that have small RGB contributions but are important for semantic prediction. Once removed, their semantic information cannot be recovered by later quantization. We propose ClunoGS, a compact framework for Language 3DGS that combines semantics-aware Gaussian sparsification and vector quantization in a unified constrained objective. Semantic supervision is used during sparsification, and the objective jointly considers rendering quality, semantic accuracy, and compactness. We optimize the unified objective with alternating primal, sparsification, quantization, and dual updates. We evaluate ClunoGS on open-vocabulary localization and segmentation using the LERF and ScanNet-10 benchmarks. Under aggressive compression, our unified, semantics-aware formulation substantially alleviates the degradation of semantic representations caused by sequential compression and semantics-agnostic Gaussian sparsification. Ablations further show that jointly coordinating sparsification and quantization better preserves semantic accuracy than applying them independently.

[678] arXiv:2610.30014 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Agent Behavior Maps: Locating Agents by What They Would Do, Without Running Them
Shota Fujikawa, Takuya Tamura, Kosuke Akimoto, Daichi Haraguchi, Masafumi Oyamada
Comments: 23 pages, 5 figures, 12 tables. Under review
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

LLM agents with similar success rates can follow different action sequences. An Agent Behavior Map represents LLM-harness combinations using centered action log-likelihoods on shared reference trajectories, without requiring new environment rollouts from the target agent. We derive error bounds relating squared coordinate distances to trajectory KL under explicit assumptions, and across eight cross-scored models the distances track the directly measured trajectory KL in rank order. Across 100 LLMs and four environments, ALFWorld-based coordinates support performance prediction and identify behavioral similarities. In ALFWorld, these similarities persist after controlling for success rates and model size, including across model families. As an extension, harness-component displacements approximately compose, with accuracy varying across components and environments.

[679] arXiv:2610.30015 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Enhancing IoT Network Reliability through Antenna Diversity in Real-World Scenarios
Marco Niederberger, Yanick Schoch, Michel A. Nyffenegger, Christian Gwerder, Hans-Dieter Lang
Comments: 5 pages, 8 figures, 1 table
Journal-ref: 2025 19th European Conference on Antennas and Propagation (EuCAP)
Subjects: Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Signal Processing (eess.SP)

Antenna diversity in Internet of Things (IoT) devices is explored to address challenges associated with fixed device orientation and interference from nearby metallic objects, which can degrade wireless network performance. Integrating multiple antennas with different polarizations can significantly enhance signal quality and network reliability. Experiments demonstrated significant improvements in link quality, with gains exceeding 30 dB in received signal strength for specific scenarios. Already the addition of a second PCB-based antenna alone, resulted in a 17 dB improvement. These findings suggest that the added complexity in hardware and software to incorporate antenna diversity could well be justified by the resulting enhancements in network stability for real-world applications.

[680] arXiv:2610.30016 [pdf, html, other]
Title: Code Comprehensor: Hierarchical Documentation and Cross-Modal Retrieval for Large Repositories
Sujoy Roychowdhury, Joseph H. R. Isaac, Jiangning Gao, Martin Klitte, Diarmuid Corcoran
Comments: Accepted at 42nd International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Understanding large, complex, and rapidly evolving code bases remains a core challenge for software engineering at scale, hindering onboarding, maintenance, refactoring, and impact analysis. Providing this information to a Large-Language Model (LLM) is another hurdle, as the LLM must understand not only the required code method but also its associated methods in the grand scheme of the repository.
