Comments: Code and model weights open-sourced
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Curating large labeled CT datasets is expensive and constrained by patient privacy. We present NV-Generate-BodyMask, a 3D latent diffusion model that synthesizes whole-body CT segmentation masks with precise, joint control over organ anatomy, tumor burden, and patient demographics. The model operates in the compressed latent space of a frozen mask autoencoder, generating $256^3$ volumetric label maps conditioned on a 19-dimensional vector via Adaptive Group Normalization and cross-attention. A size-adaptive ROI loss with spatial halo weighting and a paired tumor injection pipeline enable accurate tumor size conditioning despite the scarcity of annotated tumor cases. Trained on 8,571 masks across 26 cohorts spanning 132 labels, the model achieves Spearman $\rho = 0.70$--$0.92$ for organ size, 85--100\% tumor recall for lung, pancreatic, colon, and bone lesions, and strong demographic alignment (BMI $\rho = 0.78$, sex-conditioned perfect prostate control).

[1153] arXiv:2610.24168 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
Patrick Zhao, Yuxuan Li, Hirokazu Shirado
Subjects: Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computers and Society (cs.CY)

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the Model Capacity Frontier (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.

[1154] arXiv:2610.24291 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: An important Bottleneck in LLM Optimizers: Principle-Level Local Optima
Nian Ran, Tianhe Jia, Zhengyang Mu, Yue Wang, Sebastian Brulin, Markus Olhofer, Mauricio A. Alvarez, Yang Liu, Richard Allmendinger
Comments: 10 pages under review
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Feedback-driven LLM optimizers are increasingly used for evolutionary search, Bayesian optimization, heuristic design, and scientific discovery. Yet rapid initial gains often give way to prolonged plateaus despite substantial remaining evaluation budgets. We investigate \emph{principle-level search collapse}, where an optimizer's search becomes confined to a narrow set of design principles, even though it may continue to generate distinct candidates and achieve small improvements. We assemble a diagnostic benchmark spanning molecular optimization, network sentinel-node selection, and GPU-kernel optimization, and introduce a decision-tree protocol combining principle narrowing, prolonged performance plateaus, and gaps to attainable reference solutions. Across 161 assessable runs on the three problem domains, 78.3\% receive support for collapse, including 55.3\% with strong support. Candidate-level variation can nevertheless conceal restricted search at the principle level. We then test \emph{diversity injection}, a common response to search stagnation, such as higher t, multiple LLMs, and web search, and show that it provides limited and inconsistent benefits: among 65 molecular runs, still 73.8\% and 53.8\% receive support and strong support respectively. We finally test reference-principle interventions and find that they improve some runs, but their benefits vary across models and tasks: access to a better principle does not guarantee its effective use. Our benchmark and diagnostic protocol provide a basis for evaluating future optimizers on principle-level collapse. Our findings highlight the need for online collapse detection and better mechanisms for generating and maintaining alternative principles during optimization.

[1155] arXiv:2610.24481 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: DuoLM: Fast and Effective Personalized Recommendation with Language Models
Jiang Wu, Yutong Song, Hongbo Wang, Guanghe Cao, Jeff Lei Liang
Comments: 19 pages. Jiang Wu and Yutong Song contributed equally. v2: Added references, corrected an author name, and standardized figure fonts
Subjects: Information Retrieval (cs.IR)

Language models can make personalized recommendations from rich item content, user history, and feedback. However, evaluating many candidates with full-text inputs incurs substantial online computation and limits serving throughput. We introduce DuoLM, a framework for fast and effective personalized recommendation that integrates a compact recommendation model with an efficient serving runtime. An encoder LLM learns compact item representations for offline reuse, while a personalized ranker LLM combines them with user history and feedback for recommendation. We train both models end to end with recommendation supervision and teacher distillation. The runtime further accelerates inference through virtual token IDs for embedding access, shared history computation, and CUDA Graph replay. Benchmark results show that our framework achieves recommendation quality comparable to that of the expert teacher model. On a single H100, it delivers approximately 26,400 candidate scores per second, about $60\times$ the throughput of the teacher served with vLLM and automatic prefix caching.

[1156] arXiv:2610.24588 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Physics-Informed Koopman Learning for Data-Efficient System Identification of Automated Vehicle Dynamics
Hangyu Li, Yiming Meng, Zhaohui Liang, Yunqing Xiao, Yuxuan Chen, Bofeng Cao, Shixiao Liang, Jiaxi Liu, Haotian Shi, Xiaopeng Li
Comments: 13 pages, 9 figures. The CATS-CF dataset and code are available at this https URL
Subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY)

Understanding how a particular automated vehicle reacts to nearby traffic can improve motion prediction, control development, traffic simulation, and safety evaluation. However, commercial automated driving systems are proprietary, and single encounters may provide only a few seconds of noisy data. Standard physical models are interpretable but inflexible, whereas neural models are often data-hungry. We propose a physics-informed Koopman framework that combines a calibrated car-following law with a correction learned from the observations. A weak-form estimator learns this correction from velocity measurements integrated over time, avoiding noise-sensitive numerical differentiation. The resulting continuous-time model predicts the follower's response and provides interpretable measures of driving behavior. Experiments on OpenACC and CATS-CF evaluate 5-, 7-, and 11-second histories. Averaged over these histories, the constant-time-headway branch reduces speed prediction error by 16.0% and 15.4% on OpenACC and CATS-CF, respectively, relative to the best neural baselines. The PI-Koopman branches achieve the lowest mean speed and gap errors among the physical and neural comparators. Weak-form estimation reduces acceleration-field reconstruction error by 74.5% in noisy known-law simulations and noise-induced field perturbation by 91.6% in paired real-vehicle measurements. The same PI-Koopman system identification supports following-mode recognition with an approximately eleven-fold difference in median residual variance between human drivers and automated vehicles, and a single residual threshold achieves 85.4% balanced accuracy. The branch informed by the intelligent driver model takes a median 17 to 26 ms for identification and forecasting on the tested central processing units, supporting frequent target adaptation.

[1157] arXiv:2610.24619 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Beyond Geometric Closure: Measuring and Diagnosing Mechanical Consistency in Visual Dynamics
Qibin Gu, Yunfeng Yan
Comments: 34 pages, including supplementary material; 16 figures and 38 tables. Code: this https URL Data and spatial evaluation: this https URL Trained models: this https URL Pretrained models and continuation states: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Image and Video Processing (eess.IV)

Visual accuracy, geometric validity, and agreement with applied forces are distinct requirements for visual dynamics. We introduce a diagnostic framework that connects reaction-free SI measurements to controlled interventions on coordinate readout, training integration, and actuator response. Reference replay calibrates the measurement path, while continuous scoring exposes progress against fixed engineering targets. With three seeds per setting, we evaluate KeyCLD and CON across 343 planar assemblies at 64/256 pixels and V-JEPA + AC and LingBot-VA on 100 shared spatial test assemblies. CON reduces image MSE by 37.6%/37.2% relative to persistence, yet neither planar model attains valid native geometry. At 256 pixels, calibrated RGB replay places forecast errors far above the reference measurement floor. Exact-state KeyCLD has identical geometric pass rates under Euler and RK4 training, yet its score rises from 52.65 to 64.30 as force and energy errors decrease. In both spatial pathways, CAD/IK reconstruction restores geometry while mean actuator residuals exceed five times the engineering targets. These diagnoses distinguish coordinate correction, numerical improvement, and persistent force-response errors, guiding targeted improvements to visual dynamics.

[1158] arXiv:2610.24858 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Arbitrary-Scale Anisotropic 3D MRI Super-Resolution with Gaussian Prototypes
Aditya Rastogi, Ramon Leiser, Prateek Singh, Martha Foltyn-Dumitru, Martin Bendszus, Fabian Bamberg, Klaus Maier-Hein, Kai Schlamp, Alexander Radbruch, Gianluca Brugnara, Philipp Vollmuth
Comments: 26 pages, 6 figures, 15 tables (including appendix)
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Reducing MRI acquisition time improves patient comfort, reduces motion artefacts, and increases scanner throughput. Clinical protocols often shorten acquisitions by sacrificing spatial resolution, particularly along the slice axis. Super-resolution can recover higher-resolution images, but existing methods are typically specialised to one scale or acquisition geometry, limiting their use across heterogeneous clinical protocols. We present GSMR3D, a continuous volumetric model that reconstructs arbitrary isotropic and anisotropic resolutions with a single checkpoint per MRI contrast. It combines a learned dictionary of anisotropic 3D Gaussian prototypes with scale-conditioned frequency encoding and an exact measurement-consistency projection, keeping reconstructions consistent with the acquired low-resolution data. We train separate models on 3,731 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted and 30,254 T1-weighted brain MRI volumes from clinical and population-based cohorts. We evaluate GSMR3D against geometry-specific specialists for isotropic, in-plane, and through-plane super-resolution using reconstruction quality and downstream tasks: brain tumour segmentation, brain-metastasis detection, and brain parcellation. GSMR3D outperforms specialists at isotropic $2\times$ and achieves better LPIPS, DISTS, and FID across all geometries, although specialists retain higher PSNR in anisotropic settings. It more faithfully preserves glioma segmentations across all geometries, achieves the highest lesion sensitivity on an independent brain-metastasis cohort, and the highest brain-parcellation agreement for isotropic and in-plane reconstruction. Reconstruction takes about 6s per volume, adding little overhead relative to acquisition-time savings. GSMR3D offers a flexible approach to MRI scan-time reduction with one model per contrast across geometries while preserving information relevant to downstream tasks.

[1159] arXiv:2610.24885 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Goal Images Are Control Targets: Spatially-Grounded Goal-Image Synthesis for Robotic Manipulation
Riddhi Chatterjee, Ritish Shrirao, Kushagra Mehrotra, Viswanath Gopalakrishnan
Comments: Accepted at WACV 2027. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Goal-conditioned manipulation policies are steered by a goal image, a picture of the desired post-manipulation scene synthesized from the current observation and a language instruction. The prevailing assumption is that better image-editing quality yields better goals, so goal generators are built and compared using general image-editing metrics. We show this assumption is false. Across two independent goal-conditioned policies on CALVIN, the image editors that top aggregate editing-quality leaderboards (Gemini 3 Pro Image and GPT Image 1.5) produce worse control targets than our proposed far smaller finetuned open models, and the gap widens sharply for the multi-step (long-horizon) tasks robots actually face. A per-dimension analysis explains why. Downstream policy success is governed almost entirely by manipulation adherence (selecting the right object and the right final state; Spearman $\rho \approx 0.9$ with success), while photorealism and aesthetic fidelity, precisely where large proprietary editors excel, are uncorrelated with success ($\rho \approx 0$). This dissociation holds on both CALVIN and the real-world-aligned SIMPLER-Bridge benchmark. We then present SGE-Goal, a spatially-grounded decomposed editing framework that predicts initial and final 2D edit-region masks before goal-image synthesis. SGE-Goal turns open base models (FLUX.1 Kontext, FLUX.2 klein) into the strongest goal generators we evaluate on CALVIN, and second only to Gemini 3 Pro Image on SIMPLER-Bridge. Base models fine-tuned with SGE-Goal also hold up under chaining far better than the best proprietary editor, sustaining roughly seven times the success rate at the longest (five-step) chains. We release code, datasets, checkpoints, and a human-aligned diagnostic evaluator. Our results argue that goal generators must be selected by downstream utility, not by editing-quality leaderboards.

[1160] arXiv:2610.24899 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: HybridResearcher: Bridging the Structured-Unstructured Boundary for Deep Research Agents
Soyoung Yoon, Peiran Xu, Han Wang, Ruofan Wu, Xiaodong Yu, Feng Yan, Mohit Bansal, Debiao Li, Seung-Won Hwang, Yuxiong He, Zhewei Yao
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. Recent evaluations on benchmarks like HybridDeepResearch show that even frontier agents struggle when evidence must cross this boundary. While these benchmarks have exposed the limitation, methodologies to explicitly teach cross-source reasoning remain absent. To address this, we introduce HybridResearcher, a 4B agent trained to bridge evidence across the structured and unstructured boundary. To build it, we synthesize cross-source bridge trajectories by starting with validated single-source tasks-such as existing text-to-SQL or web search queries-and fabricating the missing source around a bridge entity drawn from the seed's own output. We retain a sample only when strict construction gates confirm that neither side alone suffices, ensuring the data requires true cross-source interdependence. Finally, we train on this curated dataset using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Evaluated on the existing HybridDeepResearch benchmark, HybridResearcher improves over our base model, Qwen3.5-4B, by 30.0 points pass@8 and surpasses the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B by 8.3 points, while also improving over its base model on established, held-out single-source benchmarks (BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus), demonstrating that this complex cross-source reasoning can be taught directly to small models without triggering catastrophic forgetting.

[1161] arXiv:2610.24930 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: TrustAgent-RFF: Agentic Diagnostic Planning for Reliable RF Fingerprinting under Domain Shift
Chuan Liu, Tianya Zhao, Yiting Wang, Junqing Zhang, Xuyu Wang
Comments: 10 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Submitted to INFOCOM
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) models can achieve accuracy under source domain conditions but become unreliable when the receiver, distance, collection day, or environment changes. Incorrect predictions in unseen domains may receive high softmax confidence, making confidence thresholding insufficient for trustworthy deployment. We propose TrustAgent-RFF, a prediction level reliability framework for RFF that operates with a frozen in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) classifier without target domain labels. For each device prediction, the framework acquires radio frequency evidence: counterfactual stability, prototype consistency, acquisition domain similarity, and signal quality. A source calibrated trust estimator combines these diagnostics with classifier confidence, prediction margin, and evidence availability indicators. Source derived lower tail penalties and cross module interactions reduce trust when diagnostic signals indicate weak support. A large language model (LLM) based planner adaptively selects the next diagnostic action based on evidence, trust state, action costs, and remaining budget. A deterministic source calibrated decision layer updates the prediction state as Accept, Reject, or Defer. Experiments across five RFF datasets and classifier backbones reveal an average source to target accuracy drop of 38.7% and show that many incorrect target domain predictions remain highly confident.

[1162] arXiv:2610.25018 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Structure-Aware Equivalence for Evaluating Autoformalized Statements
Yi Yu, Yu-Hsuan Wu, Guang Lin, Yuhui Zhang, Yuxiang Peng
Subjects: Programming Languages (cs.PL)

Evaluating autoformalized mathematical statements requires determining whether a candidate preserves the mathematical claim intended by a trusted reference. Existing methods approach this problem from complementary directions: reference-free learned evaluators estimate semantic agreement but are not constrained to a formal equivalence relation, while reference-based proof methods typically employ whole-statement logical equivalence to provide formal certificates, which is too coarse for translation fidelity and may identify mathematically unrelated statements.
We introduce Structure-Aware Equivalence (SAE), a role-preserving formal equivalence relation between syntactic and whole-statement logical equivalence that allows formally justified reformulations while preserving translation-relevant mathematical structure. We operationalize SAE in the Autoformalization Correctness Evaluator (ACE), which provides certified equivalence or inequivalence judgments and reports Inconclusive otherwise. On ProofNetVerif, a benchmark introduced with BEq+, ACE retains substantial equivalent-case coverage while remaining highly conservative in certifying disputed or inequivalent pairs. On targeted diagnostics, BEq+ accepts 94-96% of unrelated but whole-statement logically equivalent pairs, while Mathesis LeanScorer accepts 42% of localized meaning-changing perturbations; ACE accepts none of either set as equivalent.

[1163] arXiv:2610.25043 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: VLA-Rolling: Fewer Denoising Steps, Better Control via Adaptive Action Reuse
Sicheng He, Yi Pan, Qiuting Yu, Jiaming Huang, Qi Lu, Shuyan Wu, Hongyan Feng, Xuanyu Liu, Jun Zhang, Jie Zhang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang, Jianwei Yin
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Robotics (cs.RO)

Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at this https URL.

[1164] arXiv:2610.25113 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a learner-free swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
Galen J. Wilkerson
Comments: 16 pages, 9 figures, code and data: this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Social and Information Networks (cs.SI); Mathematical Physics (math-ph); Adaptation and Self-Organizing Systems (nlin.AO); Biological Physics (physics.bio-ph)

The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.

[1165] arXiv:2610.25169 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: When Is Disclosing Private Conversations with AI to the State Justified? Proactive Referral Policies of Major U.S. AI Companies through the Lens of Contextual Integrity
Minjong Cheon, Hanseon Joo, Ook Lee, Jongchang Ahn
Comments: 38 pages (22-page main text followed by 16-page supplementary material). Minjong Cheon and Hanseon Joo contributed equally
Subjects: Computers and Society (cs.CY)

AI companies engage in "proactive referral," notifying law enforcement of user conversations they judge dangerous without a government request. This poses a dilemma, since referral may expose people who merely confided dangerous thoughts to an AI to investigation, whereas not referring may leave actual violence unprevented. This study asks under what conditions proactive referral can be justified and to what extent companies' public policies disclose those conditions. Drawing on contextual integrity theory and the norms governing exceptional information sharing in confidential counseling, online posts, and private communications, the study develops eight justification criteria classified as required, presumptive, or recommended. Three evaluators analyzed 27 public documents from six major U.S. AI companies using the criteria applicable to corporate policies. No company clarified whether broad sharing provisions or narrower safety notices took precedence, and assessments of referral scope depended on which provisions were given precedence. No company disclosed the specific factual thresholds and exception conditions governing referral decisions, or whether users would be notified afterward. The study turns contextual integrity into a stage-by-stage framework for proactive referral, shows that policy documents must be read in light of their relationships, and proposes policy elements for keeping proactive referral a narrow exception disclosed in advance.

[1166] arXiv:2610.25192 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Acharya 2.0: An AI Tutor for Self-Learning Subjects in Hindi
Shantipriya Parida, Debasish Dhal, Sonal Khosla, Sambit Sekhar, Muhammed Abdur Rahmaan Kamaldeen
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Text processing is crucial for low-resource languages as it enables the development of tools and technologies that bridge the digital divide and provide equitable access to information and services. By empowering low-resource languages with robust text processing, we can preserve linguistic diversity, enhance education, improve communi- cation, and foster inclusivity in a rapidly digitizing world. Due to the lack of sufficient annotated datasets and lin- guistic resources, it is challenging to develop accurate and reliable language technologies for these low-resource languages. Large Language Models (LLMs) have attracted sig- nificant attention with their performance and the value they produce. However, with the ever-evolving language, adapting LLMs for a specific task is time-consuming and resource-intensive. Thus, Retrieval-Augmented Genera- tion (RAG) has overcome this limitation by augmenting LLMs with external knowledge, thereby improving their efficiency and extensive task-specific adaptation. Most applications of the RAG technique have been limited to English and has seen limited application in In- dic languages. This paper introduces the RAG-powered AI-Tutor application, Acharya 2.0, designed to produce academic assistance to Hindi-speaking students. The client-server-based web application integrates many fea- tures to support students in accessing and interacting with educational content.

[1167] arXiv:2610.25369 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Painting Change Map as guidance for generating painting processes
Markus Pobitzer, Chang Liu, Niccolò Biondi, Nicu Sebe
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Digital art generation has undergone a massive paradigm shift, moving from static image synthesis to dynamic video generation that can mimic the human painting process. While existing models can synthesize visually stunning time-lapses of paintings being created or "unpainted," they largely treat the creative process as a black box. Current conditioning mechanisms are either too rigid, relying on static geometric cues like Canny edges or depth maps, or too holistic, utilizing simple scalar progress variables that offer no localized control. Consequently, users lack the agency to steer how a painting evolves over time. In this work, we argue that true control over the video generation of artwork requires a joint understanding of two fundamental dimensions: where an artist acts, and when those actions take place. To achieve this, we introduce the Painting Change Map, a novel spatio-temporal control mechanism that explicitly tracks normalized structural changes across a 1,000-timestep continuum, a resolution sufficient to capture fine-grained stroke-level changes while remaining computationally tractable. By mapping localized visual differences into an encoded RGB space, our representation enables fine-grained guidance for both the forward painting and reverse unpainting processes. Extensive benchmarking demonstrates the efficacy of our approach. We outperform existing control baselines and achieve competitive or superior results compared to state-of-the-art painting methods. Furthermore, under oracle conditions, our method surpasses all baselines by a significant margin. Code is available at this https URL.

[1168] arXiv:2610.25398 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A conservative reduced collision model for the Boltzmann equation
Pei Zhang, Yanli Wang
Comments: 23 pages, 10 figures, 9 tables
Subjects: Numerical Analysis (math.NA)

The evaluation of the quadratic collision operator is one of the major computational bottlenecks in solving the Boltzmann equation owing to the high dimensionality and the nonlinear structure of the collision term. In this work, a conservative reduced collision (RC) model is developed within the discrete velocity framework. The bilinear collision operator is approximated through a kernel tensor preassembled with the problem-dependent reduced bases for the distribution function and the collision term. Consequently, online evaluation of the quadratic collision operator is reduced to tensor contractions. Exact discrete conservation of mass, momentum, and energy is enforced by constructing the collision basis in the orthogonal complement of the space spanned by the discrete collision invariants. Several numerical experiments validate the efficiency of this RC model.

[1169] arXiv:2610.25400 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: RAHF-Net: Range-Aware Heterogeneous Fusion for LiDAR-Assisted RGB Semantic Segmentation
R.D. Lin, Pengcheng Weng, Ge Wang, Han Ding, Fei Wang
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

This paper studies LiDAR-assisted RGB semantic segmentation, where LiDAR point-cloud features improve dense pixel-wise predictions in the RGB image plane rather than 3D point labels or detections. Existing 2D fusion methods often project point clouds into shallow depth/range maps and apply spatially uniform fusion, discarding rich 3D structure and ignoring the range-dependent reliability of outdoor LiDAR. We propose RAHF-Net, a Range-Aware Heterogeneous Fusion Network. Its Cylindrical-to-Perspective (C2P) module projects pretrained cylindrical voxel features into the image plane, preserving structured 3D semantic priors. A Range-Aware Heterogeneous Fusion (RAHF) module then uses a soft depth-derived range mask to perform LiDAR-guided geometric enhancement in reliable near-field regions and visual-context enhancement in sparse far-field regions. On KITTI-360, RAHF-Net achieves 65.76 mIoU, outperforming representative RGB-only and RGB-LiDAR baselines, including CMX by 1.45 points. Experiments on DELIVER further demonstrate improved robustness under adverse weather, illumination degradation, and sensor corruption.

[1170] arXiv:2610.25402 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: When Form Changes but Logic Doesn't: Building Logic-invariant LLMs through Logical Structure
Xuyuan Liu, Xinshuai Dong, Elynn Chen, Yujun Yan
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026, 24 Pages
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse reasoning tasks, yet it remains unclear whether this performance reflects an understanding of underlying logical structure or a reliance on shallow semantic cues. A key indicator of such understanding is whether models treat logically equivalent inputs consistently, producing the same predictions despite differences in expression. Through systematic evaluation on curated data, we show that even strong LLMs often fail this test: they do not consistently preserve predictions across logically equivalent inputs and generalize poorly to unseen logical forms. To address this limitation, we propose LoGIcal STructure-guided reasoning (LoGIST), a framework that guides LLM reasoning with explicit logical structure. LoGIST maps each input instance to a decision diagram, a directed acyclic graph that captures the underlying logical structure, and encodes this graph into a logical embedding that conditions the LLM's reasoning process. Across multiple training settings, LoGIST reduces inconsistency under logical equivalence and improves generalization to unseen logical forms, suggesting that logical invariance is a useful target for building more robust and generalizable logical reasoning in LLMs.

[1171] arXiv:2610.25404 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: MT Forcing: Towards Stable and Consistent Multi-Turn Image Editing with Autoregressive Diffusion
Houyuan Chen, Fanzhou Wang, Xiangyu Fan, Zesong Qiu, Yukun Wei, Songlin Yang, Zhitao Yang, Lvmin Zhang, Pei Yang, Hao Zhao, Dahua Lin, Lei Yang, Anyi Rao
Comments: Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Multi-turn image editing aims to modify an image according to a sequence of instructions, enabling more effective interactive visual content creation for users. However, existing methods often exhibit noticeable drift after only a few editing turns, manifesting in two aspects: 1) unstable visual quality, with accumulating artifacts and degraded details; and 2) inconsistent image content, with unintended changes to preserved regions and prior edits. To address these challenges, we propose MT Forcing, a novel training paradigm for multi-turn image editing with unified multimodal models (UMMs) based on autoregressive diffusion. Specifically, we propose Single-Turn Distribution Matching Distillation (Single-Turn DMD), which supervises student self-rollouts with a teacher that applies cumulative edits to the source image in a single turn, providing visual-quality guidance without recursive error accumulation. Additionally, we introduce Teacher-Forcing Guidance, which supervises history-dependent transitions on reference trajectories during warmup and as a regularizer during distillation, encouraging cross-turn content consistency beyond what per-turn distribution matching alone can ensure. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the multi-turn image editing capabilities of UMMs, yielding more stable visual quality and stronger cross-turn consistency.

[1172] arXiv:2610.25463 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: DiaLong: Benchmarking Reminiscence in Long-Context Dialogues
Owen Bianchi, Samer Aslan, Ryunosuke Saito
Comments: Equal contribution. Work conducted in 2023 at Johns Hopkins University
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

How well can transformer-based Large Language Models (LLMs) retain and recall memories in long contexts of dialogue? LLMs are known to forget long-range factual information in their context, yet the field lacks a comprehensive benchmark to quantitatively assess these shortcomings. We present DiaLong, a long-context dialogue dataset and accompanying memory task that standardizes evaluation in this space. It consists of 100 unique conversations created by humans and then augmented with LLMs, extending beyond lengths found in existing datasets. Our selected memory task is fact recall: classify 40 candidate facts about a dialogue as true or false. This task directly probes the model's ability to actively retain and retrieve information, serving as a critical measure of memory within extended conversational contexts. In testing both the latest LLMs and proposed memory enhancements on DiaLong, we demonstrate that more work needs to be done to enable LLMs with better memory performance. By enhancing memory capabilities, LLMs can improve in maintaining coherence, relevance, and human-like interaction over extended conversation. Improving these capabilities will help LLMs fulfill diverse user needs and expectations in various conversational scenarios.

[1173] arXiv:2610.25600 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Vector-Quantized World Model: Latent Feedback Motion Planning for Robot Manipulation
Xuezhou Xu, Chung-Pang Wang, Zhenzhen Li, Benjamin Riviere
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Visual world models have shown strong potential for robot planning, yet long-horizon manipulation remains challenging due to compounding prediction errors, large search complexity, and latent plans that the low-level controller cannot reliably reach. In this work, we introduce Vector-Quantized World Model (VQ-WM), a latent feedback motion planning framework that integrates discrete long-horizon search with continuous visual feedback control: a discrete latent predictor models transitions between vector-quantized latent states, allowing the planner to look far ahead and find a shortest path to the goal through discrete search and a continuous learned controller sequentially reaches the planned states through visual feedback, correcting deviations to mitigate compounding errors. Whereas most vector quantization uses Euclidean distance, we use a novel estimator of the first-passage-time as a quasi-metric, which aligns the planning abstraction with the controller's capabilities. We evaluate on the physical robot manipulation of the Tower of Hanoi puzzle: whereas existing state-of-the-art foundation models (VLAs, WAMs) only succeed when the solution trace in their training dataset, our method achieves 100\% success rate with only short-play data, demonstrate its ability to compose long-horizon solutions beyond the short demonstrated trajectories and execute them reliably. Our solution also outperforms strongest world-models by 13.3--85.3 percentage points on simulation benchmarks spanning manipulation and locomotion, demonstrating consistent progress and new capabilities.

[1174] arXiv:2610.25623 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: High Precision Multiplicative-Error Approximation of $\#$SAC$^1$ Functions in Logspace Uniform AC$^1$
Kuan Cheng, Shengtang Huang, Ruiyang Wu
Subjects: Computational Complexity (cs.CC)

Cheng and Wang (CCC' 24) showed that BPL is contained in logspace uniform AC$^1$ (denoted as L-AC$^1$). We upgrade their result by showing that approximations of $\#$SAC$^1$ functions can be computed in L-AC$^1$ with multiplicative error $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$. Previously, approximations of $\#$SAC$^1$ functions are known to be in $\mathsf{NC}^2$ via its exact computation given by Vinay (CCC' 91). A main corollary of our result is that Probabilisitic polynomial time logspace AuxPDMs and Read-$k$ logspace PTMs are computable by L-AC$^1$ with multiplicative error $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$. Notice that multiplicative error approximations are stronger than additive error approximations in the sense that they can be used to decide both non-deterministic computations and two-sided error probabilistic computations. We note that recently OpenAI announced that BPL $=$ L. Even if we only consider derandomizing probabilistic logspace, our L-AC$^1$ computation has the advantage that the error can be $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$ and can be multiplicative.

[1175] arXiv:2610.25736 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Learning from Fleet Experience: Collective Experience Learning Across 96 Robots
Chao Yu, Shu'ang Yu, Hao Lin, Hongzhi Zang, Yuxiang Yan, Chenxi Jiang, Zhen Guo, Chuankang Li, Yihao Chen, Xin Xu, Xu Fu, Jiakai Zhou, Liangzhi Shi, Hongyi Ren, Yiwei Liu, Jing Wu, Yuanqing Wang, Chen Wu, Bo Dai, Chunyu Yang, Hongliang Huang, Shuoyu Yue, Weiqi Yin, Yinuo Chen, Ruihua Chen, Chunyang Zhu, Han Xiao, Yanghao Li, Ruipu Wu, Zhikai Cai, Xiu Chen, Xu Tan, Si Liu, Yuchen Yan, Jialin Zhang, Wen Zeng, Yiming Zhou, Zixiao Huang, Xinlei Chen, Guanghui Ren, Quanlu Zhang, Boxun Li, Maoqing Yao, Yu Wang
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Robot deployment generates experience that can support policy improvement, but continued reliance on expert corrective actions makes learning difficult to scale across growing fleets. We propose learning from fleet experience: using deployed robots' own executions as a source of supervision for further policy improvement. We call this paradigm Collective Experience Learning (CEL), in which robots pool execution experience to update a shared policy that returns to the fleet. Following expert-supervised initialization, we realize CEL through failure-guided experience retrieval fine-tuning (FERT). FERT uses failure contexts to retrieve relevant segments from successful trajectories and prioritizes their recorded actions for supervised updates, without collecting additional expert demonstrations or corrective actions. Operators provide binary episode-outcome labels and environment resets. A fault-tolerant asynchronous training system (FATS) coordinates robot execution, cloud inference and policy optimization despite local interruptions. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, the resulting policies achieve success rates of 93.3-99.2%, evaluated over 120 trials per task on robots excluded from training data collection. With collection time per robot held fixed, larger fleets provide more experience and generally improve performance across the evaluated sizes. On multi-stage phone packaging, learning with 96 robots raises success from 79.2% to 98.3%. These results support CEL as a scalable approach to improving robot policy reliability through experience generated during deployment.

[1176] arXiv:2610.25841 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Union of Translates of a Convex Body
Alec Shelley, Daniel Tartakovsky
Comments: 27 pages, 5 figures; v2 updated abstract
Subjects: Computational Geometry (cs.CG); Metric Geometry (math.MG)

Let $K\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a strictly convex body and let $Z\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ be a finite set of sites in general position. We consider the problem of calculating the volume $\mu_d$ of $\bigcup_{z\in Z}(z-K)$. Let $V_z$ be the Voronoi cell of $z\in Z$ with respect to the convex distance function induced by $K$, and let $N$ be the nerve of the Voronoi cells. When $K$ is a ball, a classical result reduces the inclusion-exclusion formula to a sum over $N$: $\mu_d(\bigcup_{z\in Z}(z-K))=\sum_{J\in N}(-1)^{|J|+1}\mu_d(\bigcap_{z\in J}(z-K))$. When may the hypothesis that $K$ is a ball be dropped? We show that for $d\leq 2$ the reduced formula holds for every strictly convex $K$, while for each $d\geq 3$ there is a strictly convex $K$ for which it fails. For $x\in\mathbb{R}^d$, let $\chi_x$ be the Euler characteristic of the subcomplex of $N$ induced by the sites lying in $K+x$. A sufficient condition for the reduced formula to hold is $\chi_x\equiv 1$ on the union. When $d=3$ and $K$ is $C^4$, we show that $\chi_x\equiv 1$ on the union for all $Z$ in general position if and only if $K$ is an ellipsoid. The proof relies on the Fubini-Pick affine invariant.

[1177] arXiv:2610.25960 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: HORIA: 4D Human and Object Reconstruction from a Monocular Video with Interaction-Aware Re-Rendering
Hyeongjin Nam, Taeryung Lee, Daniel Sungho Jung, Kyoung Mu Lee
Comments: 17 pages including the supplementary material
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Joint 4D reconstruction of a human and object from a monocular video is essential for understanding how people interact with their environment. While recent methods have made noticeable progress, capturing such human-object interactions remains difficult due to two main challenges. First, a video typically contains composite semantic context spanning multiple interaction phases, making it difficult to track the temporal changes of the interaction in the reconstruction. Second, under human-object occlusion, a single-view observation contains incomplete visual information about the interaction, resulting in geometrically inconsistent reconstructions. To address these challenges, we introduce HORIA, built upon two core designs. First, we decompose the entire input video into temporally grounded and semantically distinct interaction phases with motion-aware captioning, obtaining a specific text description for each phase. Second, conditioned on these text descriptions of the interaction, we propose an interaction-aware re-rendering that compensates for the limited single-view observation. Specifically, we render the initially reconstructed 4D human and object from novel viewpoints and refine the renderings with a text-to-video diffusion prior, which provides auxiliary novel-view supervision beyond single-view cues. As a result, our framework produces temporally coherent and accurate 4D reconstructions under diverse interaction scenarios, achieving state-of-the-art performance.

[1178] arXiv:2610.25961 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: PaceVLA: Adaptive Temporal Action Quantization in Vision-Language-Action Models
Hojin Jeon, Jimin Lee, Taekwan Kim, Nayoung Oh, Taeyoung Kim, Myungkyu Koo, Jinmo Koo, Joonwoo Ahn, Jinwoo Shin
Comments: 25 pages, 7 figures, 10 tables. Project page: this https URL
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Fast and reliable manipulation is crucial for practical robot deployment. Although Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently shown remarkable progress as generalist robot policies, their execution often remains temporally inefficient. A key source of this inefficiency is that policies learn fine-grained temporal patterns from teleoperated demonstrations, requiring many low-level action steps. Temporal action quantization offers a simple way to accelerate execution by aggregating consecutive low-level actions into temporally coarser actions. However, applying action quantization without considering when fine-grained control is required introduces a speed-accuracy trade-off: accelerated actions may efficiently reduce redundant steps in some phases, while discarding critical motion details in precision-sensitive interactions. To address this, we propose PaceVLA, a unified framework for adaptive temporal execution in VLAs that integrates two coupled components: (1) mode-specific action decoders built on a shared action expert, supporting multiple temporal granularities and prediction horizons, and (2) a quantizability-guided mode selection scheme which decides whether coarse execution is appropriate, and a context-conditioned router that selects an execution mode at each inference step. Experiments across three multi-task simulation benchmarks and six real-world tasks show that PaceVLA improves execution efficiency while maintaining task success rate across multiple embodiments, including long-horizon and dexterous manipulation.

[1179] arXiv:2610.25988 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: SSIO: Self-Supervised Inertial Odometry
Yuheng Qiu, Yutian Chen, Carlton Cort, Weison Huang, Shibo Zhao, Pieter Abbeel, Rocky Duan, Koushil Sreenath, C. Karen Liu, Carmelo Sferrazza, Junyi Geng, Sebastian Scherer, Guanya Shi
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Learning inertial odometry for a new platform usually requires ground-truth trajectories. We show that an inertial odometry model can instead be trained from scratch by a myopic teacher that integrates the IMU over each short window independently, a scheme we call integration self-supervision. Interestingly, although supervised only by short-window velocity changes, the student learns to directly predict velocity, and does so more accurately than its integration teacher. Pose graph distillation then refines the model with sequence-consistent targets from a pose graph over many windows. Training on a new platform therefore no longer requires collecting ground-truth trajectories, but only calibrating the IMU and recording data during normal operation. Across six datasets spanning pedestrians, drones, quadrupeds, and a humanoid, the same recipe with no velocity or position labels trains models that come within 0.07~m/s average velocity error of a same-architecture supervised baseline.

[1180] arXiv:2610.26255 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: XGLASS: X-Ray, Gaze and Language Assisted Slice Sequencing for CT Volumes
Michael Glöckler, Timo Ropinski
Comments: Accepted at WACV 2027. 24 pages, including references and supplementary material. Code and checkpoint: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Vision-language models (VLMs) achieve remarkable performance on 2D medical images, such as X-rays or pathology images, while 3D VLMs that directly process CT/MRI volumes lag behind due to limited 3D training data and the predominance of 2D foundation architectures. To leverage powerful 2D VLMs for analyzing medical volumes, which contain hundreds of slices, it is therefore necessary to focus only on those few slices, which are diagnostically relevant. To enable such a prioritization, we propose XGLASS, a method that transfers medical expertise from 2D X-rays to 3D CT for task-aware slice prioritization. XGLASS uses disease-conditioned importance maps derived from language-aligned radiologist gaze on X-rays and spatially aligns them with coronal CT projections, bringing gaze priors and CT content into a shared 2D representation. The fused gaze-prior/CT projection is then used to predict a disease-specific ordering of axial slices, prioritizing diagnostically relevant slices. XGLASS significantly improves budgeted retrieval over 2D and 3D-native baselines, achieving a top-10 hit rate up to 75.9% for the best-performing disease. In practice, this means that after inspecting only the top 10 slices (4.17% of a 240-slice scan), XGLASS identifies a diagnostically relevant slice in more than 75% of cases. For downstream slice-wise finding classification, an XGLASS-selected 30-slice candidate set reduces model calls by 87.5% while improving F1 by 11.3 percentage points over all-slice inference, 4.2 points over the strongest 2D selector, and remains competitive with 3D-native selectors while requiring up to 130.8 times less time and 10.9 times less GPU memory per finding, supporting its use as a lightweight preselector for volumetric CT analysis. The code and pretrained checkpoint are available on this https URL.

[1181] arXiv:2610.26261 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge
Wanli Ma, Tianmeng Hu, Ke Li
Comments: 20 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.

[1182] arXiv:2610.26390 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Cartender: Verifiable Language-Conditioned Driving by Learning the Drives Not Taken
Zhiwen Chen, Benjin Zhu, Yan Xie, Jun Ma
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Every driving scene is logged once, but driving is one-to-many: the scene determines which behaviors are feasible, while an instruction selects among them. A log records only the action taken, leaving no direct supervision for alternative feasible actions or instructions the scene cannot support. Consequently, a policy that ignores language and one that follows it without regard to scene constraints can fit the same data. We present Cartender, which learns from the drives not taken. Counterfactual Branching constructs matched and mismatched instruction-action pairs from real recordings without a simulator: a vision-language model proposes alternative futures and their selecting instructions, while unsupported instructions provide negative labels. A learned scene-language compatibility score regulates language conditioning in trajectory generation, and a reward-trained language residual re-ranks generated candidates over a scene-based score. The branches are used for training; instruction following is evaluated by swapping instructions under identical recorded inputs and measuring behavior rather than agreement with generated targets. On WOD-E2E, the best of four proposals achieves an RFS of 8.642 across 3,603 feasible instruction conditions. Across 8,974 admitted proposals, mean RFS is 8.203 versus 7.906 for matched logged trajectories, and 67% score higher than their logged counterpart. Compared with matched-only imitation using the same backbone, Cartender improves same-scene paired instruction success from 23.67% to 57.00% and RFS from 6.32 to 7.10; its gate reduces infeasible-instruction execution from 53.36% to 14.18%.

[1183] arXiv:2610.26453 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Learning What to Remember: Resource-Efficient Self-Improvement for Lifelong Agents
Guannan Lai, Zi-Yang Bai, Jun-Peng Jiang, Han-Jia Ye
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Self-improving agents aim to continuously improve their behavior by learning from experience after deployment. However, accumulating and reusing more experience does not necessarily lead to better decisions, particularly when generation, interaction, and memory resources are jointly constrained. Under such stringent constraints, we find that several existing lifelong-memory methods provide limited benefits over simple retrieval or even no-memory agents. This reveals a fundamental challenge for resource-efficient self-improvement: agents must learn not only which past experiences are relevant, but which are actually worth reusing to improve future decisions. When memory capacity and opportunities for reasoning and recovery are limited, retrieving an ineffective experience can consume scarce resources and hinder downstream execution. To address this challenge, we propose TokenWorth, a lightweight feedback-driven memory adaptation framework that learns query-dependent memory worth from sparse execution feedback. Without updating the backbone model, TokenWorth uses the learned worth to guide both experience retrieval and bounded memory management, enabling the agent to continually adapt how it reuses accumulated experience. Across three LifelongAgentBench environments and both local and API-based deployments, TokenWorth achieves the highest task success rate while using the fewest output tokens among the evaluated methods under the specified resource budgets. These results suggest that effective self-improvement under resource constraints depends not on accumulating more experience, but on learning what is worth remembering. Our code is publicly available at this https URL.

[1184] arXiv:2610.26496 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Mitigating Reward Hacking in Preference Reward Models with Evolving Penalties
Afonso Baldo, António Farinhas, Marcos Treviso, Ricardo Rei, Nuno M. Guerreiro
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Reinforcement learning for language models has moved from preference reward models to verifiable rewards, which sustain much longer optimization. Preference models are prone to reward hacking: the policy raises their score without improving response quality, or even while degrading it. Yet for open-ended tasks, where quality can neither be verified nor fully written down as rubrics, they remain valuable. We introduce Dynalize, which mitigates reward hacking online, during policy training. Periodically and asynchronously, a language model analyzes training rollouts and writes penalties for undesirable behaviors that the reward model appears to reward; a judge applies them to every rollout. In clinical counseling and creative writing, training on the reward model alone raises its score continuously but ultimately leads to a decline in external benchmarks; Dynalize sustains longer training and results in improved downstream performance. We find that our method suppresses patterns incentivized by preference models that, without penalties, spread to most responses, and even to the model's reasoning, which the reward model does not explicitly score. Furthermore, we show that its gains hold in multi-turn training, and even after we retrain the reward model on the discovered behaviors.

[1185] arXiv:2610.26538 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Small Average Error, Wide Individual Error: General-Purpose LLMs Estimating Energy Intake from Meal Photos in a Feeding Trial
Xiaomeng Li
Comments: 20 pages, 1 figure, 12 tables. v2: adds Gemini 3.8 Flash and Gemini 4 Argon under a pre-registered addendum; all tables recomputed over eight models; conclusions unchanged except that one model now meets the pre-set limits of agreement, narrowly. Code, prompts, per-meal model outputs: this https URL
Subjects: Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Quantitative Methods (q-bio.QM)

Photo-based estimation of food energy could ease dietary assessment, and general-purpose multimodal large language models (LLMs) make such estimates easy to obtain. Most evaluations use one photo taken before eating and compare with energy served, while dietary assessment needs energy eaten. We evaluated eight models from three vendors (Claude Haiku, Sonnet and Opus 5.5; GPT-6 luna, 6.1 sol and 6 astra; Gemini 3.8 Flash and 4 Argon) on 802 meals from ACETADA, a controlled feeding trial with weighed intake, with the before photo only, before and after photos in separate calls (subtraction), or both photos in one request. Three results ran against intuition. Subtraction under-estimated intake for six of eight models, because the models still report hundreds of kilocalories for a nearly empty tray. Scaling the before-only estimate by the average share eaten (0.87) matched much of the gain from the after photo; beyond that constant, the second photo lowered meal-level error by only 2.2 to 4.4 points, mainly in meals with food left. With one photo, two models had a near-zero intake bias only because they under-estimated the served energy and ignored uneaten food. In ablations, adding the after photo improved accuracy under both prompt formats for seven models, while prompt effects varied across models. Over 148 feeding days, five models kept the 90% confidence interval of their mean error within a pre-set 10% margin; one model also met the pre-set 30% limits of agreement, narrowly (-28% to +27%; limits outside 30% cannot be excluded), and the other seven did not. Protein was under-estimated by every model, most in protein-dense meals; repeated calls changed error by at most 1.4 points; a high reasoning effort helped only the smallest model. A low average bias is not evidence of accurate individual intake estimation; such estimates should support, not replace, assessment by a dietitian.

[1186] arXiv:2610.26722 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Copying Under Repetition: From Prefix Matching to Position Hashing
Anxin Guo, Tianlong Huang, Chenxiao Yang, Zhiyuan Li
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Frontier LLMs can copy random text almost flawlessly, yet they often overrun or truncate long blocks of repeated characters. In repeated strings, matching local content no longer reliably identifies where copying should continue or when it should stop. Nevertheless, we show that a two-layer transformer with $O(\log\log N)$-bit precision and $O(\log N/\log\log N)$ width can copy every string up to a chosen design horizon $N$ and terminate correctly under arbitrary repetition. We use RoPE-style rotations of attention values and outputs (VO-rotations) with small prime periods to encode distances from delimiter anchors modulo those primes. By the Chinese Remainder Theorem, these periodic encodings jointly distinguish all required distances, allowing one retrieval rule to select either the next source token or the end marker. In contrast, we prove a width-independent impossibility result for copying under sequential finite-precision softmax accumulation. It applies to transformers whose only positional input is an additive attention bias that eventually becomes constant, including NoPE and a recursive implementation of ALiBi. Once an identical-token run exceeds the resulting saturation threshold, further repetitions leave the logits unchanged. If this threshold grows sublinearly with $N$, these models cannot both complete a long all-identical copy and stop correctly, a pattern resembling the termination errors of frontier LLMs. In synthetic copying experiments, baseline transformer models fail on long repeated strings even within the training range. Trained VO models, by contrast, generalize beyond the training lengths with near-perfect accuracy up to length $\approx5005$, the selected primes' period product.

[1187] arXiv:2610.26821 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: AfriBED: a Speech Recognition Bias Evaluation Dataset for Low Resource African Languages
Claytone Sikasote, Hussein Suleman, Jan Buys
Comments: Accepted at IEEE SLT 2026 Workshop Demo Track
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition systems (ASR), current systems exhibit speaker-attribute bias, i.e., their speech recognition performance is biased against certain speakers based on their demographic attributes such as gender, accents, and speaker type. However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. In this paper, we introduce African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset (AfriBED), a novel speech recognition bias evaluation dataset for two low resource African languages, Bemba and Nyanja, to detect and estimate gender and speaker-type bias for ASR systems. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.

[1188] arXiv:2610.26854 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Physical Words: A Vocabulary for Structuring Latent Reasoning in Robot Manipulation
Jiaming Liu, Xinghao Zhu, Yiming Zhang, Shanghang Zhang, Yinxi Wang, Yichu Yang, Zhuoyang Liu, Dantong Niu, Soha Pouya, Juekun Li, Yan Chang
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO)

Multimodal reasoning provides robotic foundation models with predictive context needed for reliable action generation. However, language-based reasoning captures task semantics but struggles to express fine-grained physical dynamics, while latent reasoning models future state evolution but offers limited structure for organizing these dynamics into reusable reasoning primitives. To bridge this gap, we introduce PhysWord, a reasoning-before-acting foundation model built on Physical Words, which use atomic action verbs as shared semantic anchors for continuous representations of physical dynamics. Specifically, PhysWord predicts upcoming atomic action words and directly aligns their contextual hidden states with latent targets derived from the corresponding future observations. Building on these primitives, we construct a temporally structured PhysWord space with visual and optional tactile variants of each action word. Autoregressively predicting Physical Words across future timesteps captures transitions between execution stages, providing structured multimodal context for action generation. PhysWord achieves state-of-the-art success rates of 90.3\% on visuotactile UniVTAC and 99.6\% on vision-based LIBERO-Long, and outperforms competing methods on real-world tasks using bimanual grippers and dexterous hands. Further evaluations demonstrate that our structured latent reasoning framework generalizes to unseen scenarios and enables long-horizon manipulation. Project page: this https URL

[1189] arXiv:2610.26867 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: WaveCommitments: Private and Verifiable Speech-Agent Marketplaces
Oguzhan Baser, Kaan Kale, Sriram Vishwanath, Sandeep Chinchali
Comments: 5 pages
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Multiagent Systems (cs.MA); Sound (cs.SD)

Modern speech systems are evolving into ecosystems of autonomous speech agents that interact, negotiate, and trade assets such as embeddings, spectrograms, or raw data. In such markets, sellers cannot reveal assets for evaluation due to privacy constraints, and buyers cannot price what they cannot test. Thus, we introduce WaveCommitments, an end-to-end design that couples multivariate polynomial commitments with confidential asset valuation via Data Shapley inside a trusted execution environment. It enables selective openings and tamper-evident provenance to prove that a delivered asset matches the valuation while hiding everything else. Our extensive experiments across three standard datasets and various tasks with state-of-the-art encoders, including Whisper, reveal that we speed up the strongest baselines by up to 18.1x while reducing their proof sizes by up to 43.2x. We also analyze how a speaker's value shifts across tasks and encoders, revealing agent-level market prices.

[1190] arXiv:2610.26950 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Beyond Policy Discrepancy: Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
Xuanfeng Yang, Le Gai, Jiaming Wang, Xuan Zhang
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) integrates domain specialists into a shared student, but determining how strongly each teacher should supervise remains challenging. Existing discrepancy-based allocation can assign strong supervision even when the student already matches or exceeds the teacher's task performance, since behavioral mismatch does not necessarily imply a remaining capability deficit. We propose Capability-Aware Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation (CA-MOPD), which combines specialist merging with capability-guided allocation to account for what the student has already learned. CA-MOPD first merges reinforcement-learning specialists into a strong student initialization, then uses verifier-estimated teacher--student capability gaps to adjust domain-level distillation strength. Supervision decreases as capability gaps close and increases when estimated student capability regresses, while dense token-level guidance remains provided by the teachers. Across six benchmarks spanning mathematics, code generation, and instruction following, CA-MOPD achieves an average score of 32.22, outperforming naive MOPD, Open-MOPD, and the merged initialization by 0.86, 0.83, and 0.74 points, respectively. Controlled comparisons further support the benefits of merged initialization and capability-gap guidance under matched training budgets.

[1191] arXiv:2610.27216 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Optimal Algorithms and Hardness for Max-Cut in Bounded Degree Graphs
Rares-Darius Buhai, Suprovat Ghoshal, Neng Huang, Pravesh Kothari, Euiwoong Lee, Konstantin Makarychev, Yury Makarychev
Comments: 70 Pages
Subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS)

We give a polynomial-time algorithm that achieves an $\alpha_{GW} + \tilde{\Omega}(1/d)$-approximation for Max 2-LIN(2) in weighted instances where each vertex appears in at most $d$ constraints. This improves on the $\alpha_{GW}+\tilde{\Omega}(1/d^2)$-approximation guarantee of [Hsieh-Kothari, ICALP'23]. We also show a matching Unique Games hardness under randomized polynomial-time reductions, thereby proving that the gain on $\alpha_{GW}$ is optimal up to $\mathrm{polylog}(d)$ factors. Here, $\alpha_{GW} \approx 0.878$ is the approximation ratio of the Goemans-Williamson algorithm. Our results resolve an open question due to Raghavendra and refute his conjectured optimal approximation ratio of $\alpha_{GW} + \tilde{\Omega}(1/\sqrt{d})$.
Our local improvement scheme can be thought of as using an adaptive (based on the neighbors) shift applied to the Gaussian before using the GW sign rounding. This allows us to implement a ``soft but simultaneous'' flipping decision at each vertex as opposed to hard but sequential flipping decisions in prior works. Our hardness results are based on a new sparsification lemma for graphs produced by the reduction from Unique Games [Khot-Kindler-Mossel-O'Donnell, SICOMP'07] that preserves the optimal values up to a factor of $1 \pm \epsilon$ while subsampling to an average degree of only $\tilde{O}(1/\epsilon)$. This is the first example of a CSP in which the optimal advantage on degree-$d$ instances is asymptotically smaller than $O(1/\sqrt{d})$ [Trevisan, STOC'01]. A key idea in the proof of our sparsification theorem establishes new bounds on the number of ``nearly optimal'' cuts in the output of the KKMO reduction. This step, in turn, relies on a new, robust inverse Majority-Is-Stablest theorem.

[1192] arXiv:2610.27241 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Predicting Linear Relational Decodability Without the Relation
Jonas Rohweder, Adrian Mülthaler, Faridoun Mehri, Sebastian Gerstner, Hinrich Schütze
Comments: 19 pages. v2: metadata correction (author name, abstract formatting)
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL)

Linear relational embeddings (LREs) approximate a language model's subject-to-object mapping with an affine function. Their faithfulness varies enormously across relations, from near zero for person_father to the ceiling for country_capital_city. We investigate the factors that contribute to this variation and demonstrate that it can be significantly predicted from a readout that is not aware of the underlying relation. To do so, we propose a novel form of the Jacobian lens, the entity lens. Whereas the Jacobian lens is estimated across all tokens and concepts, the entity lens EL_t is trained to predict what the model will output for an entity of type t under the neutral prompt "{} is known for"; e.g., we train ELs for countries and persons. After estimating an entity lens, we measure how highly it ranks the model's answer for a relation without using any relation-specific information in estimation and prediction. Across 28 relations of the LRE dataset on Olmo-3-7B this relation-agnostic score correlates with LRE faithfulness at $\rho = 0.7355$ (p < .01). This suggests that linear decodability is largely a property of what a subject's representation already carries, rather than of the relation being decoded. Moving the unit of analysis from the relation to the individual fact, we conclude that new relation datasets and analysis methods are needed to address several problems in existing datasets, most prominently semantically weak first tokens (e.g., most predicted universities' first token is "University") and reference competition (e.g., the LLM confuses obscure actor names with competing non-actor entities that have the same last name). Our full pipeline is available at this https URL

[1193] arXiv:2610.27264 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Theorem prover Arend
Fedor Part, Valery Isaev, Sergey Sinchuk
Subjects: Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

This paper is an exposition of the theorem prover Arend developed at JetBrains Research. Arend language has been designed to facilitate the formalization of mathematics within the framework of univalent foundations and with the focus on constructive mathematics. It is based on a variant of homotopy type theory with cubical syntax that is more closely aligned with Martin-Löf Type Theory (MLTT) than fully computational cubical type theories, while still retaining some of their computational properties useful in practice. Among the most notable features of the Arend language is its powerful system of classes and records supporting subsumptive subtyping, partial implementations and anonymous extensions, which provides extensive flexibility for constructing hierarchies of definitions. Formalization in Arend is streamlined by the IntelliJ Arend plugin, which transforms IntelliJ IDEA into a full-fledged integrated development environment (IDE) for the Arend language. The main Arend library arend-lib includes formalizations in constructive algebra, topology and synthetic homotopy theory.

[1194] arXiv:2610.27307 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Evolving Self-tuning Benchmarks for Long-Horizon Tool Use
Hyunji Alex Nam, Michael Dennis, Natasha Jaques, Minsuk Chang
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

For AI assistants to move beyond simple chat interfaces and reliably assist users with applications like Gmail, Venmo, and Slack, we need to improve their tool-use capabilities. However, existing tool use benchmarks are still limited and difficult to scale because they rely on human supervision or are too domain-specific. To make data generation scalable, we propose, TURTLE (Tool Use Related Tasks with Long-Horizon Evolution), an Unsupervised Environment Design (UED) approach to evolve existing tasks using a proposer, a solver, and a feedback generator large language model agents. The proposer is rewarded for difficult yet solvable tasks based on the solver's empirical performance, and the feedback generator summarizes the solver's execution traces for the proposer to exploit. TURTLE produces evolving, self-tuning test suites adaptable to different environment requirements, from supporting user simulators and dense document retrieval to interacting across multiple apps. Empirical results on AppWorld, $\tau$-Bench, and AutomationBench using Gemma 4 31B-it show that the evolved tasks target the desired difficulty range (e.g., a 165% increase in the percentage of hard tasks on AppWorld), increase task diversity (in terms of reasoning and simultaneous tool interactions), and elicit a broader range of failure modes than the original tasks.

[1195] arXiv:2610.27371 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: M3D-FLOW: A Monolithic 3-D-Stackable Processing-Near-DRAM Architecture for Generative Normalizing Flow Applications
Bipin Thapa Magar, Ishan Thakkar, Sudeep Pasricha
Comments: 13 pages, 12 figures. Presented in CASES 2026 as a part of ESWEEK 2026. Accepted for publication in IEEE TCAD
Subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Emerging Technologies (cs.ET)

Normalizing Flows (NFs) have shown strong results in generative modeling, recently reaching state-of-the-art image generation performance. However, their repetitive, sequential operations limit the computational and memory efficiency achievable with GPUs and TPUs. We propose M3D-FLOW, a novel monolithic 3D-stackable (M3D) DRAM-based processing-near-memory (PNM) architecture that eliminates memory bottlenecks using a Cu-Cu hybrid-bonded logic die integrated with an M3D DRAM die. The M3D DRAM provides dense bank integration and a tiered organization with variable access latencies that M3D-FLOW exploits for the efficient processing of different NF workloads. To maximize compute density while minimizing area, energy, and thermal overhead, M3D-FLOW employs hybrid binary--stochastic floating-point multipliers, performing mantissa multiplication in the stochastic domain and exponent operations in the binary domain. A pipelined execution strategy maps sequential NF stages across dynamically partitioned PE groups, and together with the stochastic hardware, enables M3D-FLOW to achieve at least $6.6\times$ higher performance and $3\times$ better energy efficiency than prior PNM accelerators, with only a 2.2% bits-per-dimension (BPD) increase over bfloat16 and 4.1% over FP32. An analysis of stochastic hardware variants further shows that shorter stochastic bitstreams reduce execution time by up to $3.3\times$ at the cost of higher approximation error, providing a concrete design guide for latency--accuracy trade-offs.

[1196] arXiv:2610.27548 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Human-Computer Interaction (cs.HC)

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants.
